s.73ce5eee83c6c15c: The six letters are gathered in the word yarmaloon: ya, ra, meem, lam, waw and nun. With ya, nun, meem and waw the merge keeps a nasal hum; with lam and ra it does not. The term also covers any two identical or close letters running together, as when a word ending in dal meets a word beginning with dal.
s.5e7575e07c2d73d2: Idghaam · Idgam · Edgham · Idghaam rules · Idgham with ghunnah · Yarmaloon
s.58daf4cc104081b6: Breaking the fast at sunset, traditionally with dates and water before the Maghrib prayer.
s.12654dad8851e683: The Prophet hastened it rather than delaying it, and said people remain in good as long as they do so. He broke his fast with fresh dates, or dry dates, or else a drink of water. Feeding a fasting person their iftar is described as earning the same reward as their fast, which is the origin of the communal iftar tables.
s.aee6315328a17271: Iftaar · Eftar · Fitoor · Iftari · Roza kushai · breaking fast
s.0773d16ef7329f98: The sanctified state a pilgrim enters with intention and talbiyah, marked by simple unsewn dress.
s.ff6461d5e54fbe83: The root means to make something forbidden, because entering it makes ordinary permissible things off limits. Men wear two unsewn white cloths; women wear ordinary modest clothing with the face and hands uncovered, and there is no special ihram dress for them. The common misunderstanding is that the towels are the ihram; they are not, and a person who has made the intention is in ihram whatever they happen to be wearing.
s.de87c53db7959e73: Ehram · Ihraam · Ahram · Ihram clothes · Ihram state · two white cloths
s.77186147d0cbb88d: To worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, knowing that He sees you.
s.9b020697aa3cf45d: The definition is the Prophet's own wording in the hadith of Jibril, collected in Bukhari and Muslim. The word means to do a thing beautifully, and it reaches past worship into how a person treats people and animals. It is the difference between a prayer performed and a prayer attended.
s.e1bcb2c2c146afa8: Ehsan · Ihsaan · Ehsaan · Excellence in worship · Excellence · Perfection of worship
s.eeb2136d3a6e2a17: Hire or lease: paying for the use of something, or for another person's labour.
s.61f70ff8fa233ebe: The Qur'an mentions hiring a worker in the story of Musa in Madyan and instructs that a nursing mother be paid her due. The contract needs a defined benefit, a defined period and a known wage agreed in advance. The reported instruction to give the worker his wage before his sweat dries is the most quoted line in the whole chapter. In Islamic finance, ijarah is the leasing structure used in place of an interest bearing loan.
s.657a1aa68d2f3ff4: Ijara · Ijaarah · Ejarah · Icare · Ijarah muntahia · Ajir
s.0b75959cd5451e1a: A teacher's licence permitting a student to transmit a text or a collection onward.
s.f1c9ceff8a549921: An ijazah is a link in a living chain: the holder can say he received this book from his teacher, who received it from his, back to the author. It is weaker than hearing every word in person, and scholars debated how much weight it carries on its own. It is still issued today, most often for the Qur'an and for the six books.
s.6a6d12828a64410c: Ijaza · Ijazat · Icazet · Idjaza · Ejaza · Ijazah sanad
s.00412e12e8bd0690: A licence to teach a reading, granted after reciting the entire Qur'an to a qualified teacher.
s.21eaae361980b0bc: The teacher listens to every letter, corrects it, and only then names the student in an unbroken chain of teachers reaching back to the Prophet. It certifies that you were heard, not that you passed a written exam. Most ijazahs given today are in Hafs from Asim, though teachers of the other readings still grant them.
s.d924a1091c67b017: Ijazah · Ijaza · Ejaza · Ijazat · Ijazah Quran · Sanad
s.5e800acdca02d577: The agreement of the qualified scholars of one generation on a single ruling.
s.6153a8ef60024365: It is the third of the four agreed sources, after the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Certain ijma' is rare, and mostly concerns matters everyone already knows, such as the five daily prayers and the prohibition of wine. Scholars differ over whether a consensus after the Companions can ever be verified across a scattered world, so a claim of ijma' is something to check rather than accept on sight.
s.ebe78fe79fb619b9: Ijma · Ijmaa · Ijma al-ummah · Icma · Ijema · Ijmah
s.b171c787c326d5e5: The disciplined effort of a qualified scholar to derive a ruling from the sources.
s.3635848f40e06aa1: The root means to exert oneself to the limit. It applies where the texts are not decisive, since nobody performs ijtihad against a clear and settled ruling. Classical scholars set demanding conditions for the mujtahid, including Arabic, command of the Qur'an and hadith, and knowledge of where consensus lies. The Prophet taught that one who judges by ijtihad and is right has two rewards, and one who tries sincerely and is wrong still has one.
s.754c15383fa59c1a: Ictihad · Ijtehad · Ijthihad · Ijtihaad · Mujtahid · Mujtahed
s.ff927c9423119cb6: Hiding a nun sakinah or tanwin: not clear, not merged, held with a nasal hum for two counts.
s.cd3eee41c05dbfeb: It applies before fifteen letters, the ones left once the letters of izhar, idgham and iqlab are taken out. The tongue moves towards the position of the coming letter without quite touching, and the sound rests in the nose. There is a related lip rule, ikhfa shafawi, for a silent meem followed by ba.
s.bb25f2d0ef9dc2b2: Ikhfaa · Ikhfa' · Ekhfa · Ikhfa haqiqi · Ikhfaa rules · Ikhfa shafawi
s.bb89a0b8d1aaacfa: Doing an act for Allah alone, with no eye on who else is watching.
s.ff884943fa6dac39: The word means to make something pure, with nothing mixed into it. The Qur'an says people were commanded only to worship Allah, sincerely devoting religion to Him (Qur'an 98:5), and the Prophet peace be upon him said actions are only by intentions, in Bukhari and Muslim. Ikhlas is not a feeling you generate before an act. It is what is left of the act when the praise does not arrive.
s.43feb7cfb42f70cd: Ikhlaas · Iklas · Ikhlass · Ekhlas · Ihlas · Sincerity
s.ac33a11fb04ee9e5: Scholarly disagreement, which classical Islam treated as normal rather than as a crisis.
s.a93ffbec672c8686: It arises from the wording of texts, the strength of reports, differing methods, and different local customs. Scholars distinguished tolerated disagreement, where each side holds real evidence, from disagreement over what is definitively known, which is not tolerated. The Companions themselves differed and still prayed behind one another, and the standard etiquette is to act on the view you follow without condemning someone who follows another qualified one.
s.e82ac7342713a4d2: Ikhtilaaf · Ihtilaf · Ikhtelaf · Khilaf · Khilafiyyah · Ikhtilaf al-fuqaha
s.b4baffbc23de6c72: Human choice: real enough to be answerable for, and never outside Allah's knowledge and creation.
s.ef13b9b83fbb0a56: Two old errors sit on either side of the road. The Jabriyyah said a person is compelled, like a feather in wind; the Qadariyyah said a person creates his own acts independently of Allah's decree. Ahl al-Sunnah hold both truths together: Allah creates the act, and the servant genuinely chooses and earns it, a position the Ash'aris call kasb.
s.f27694ce54bd5708: Ikhtiyaar · Free will · Freewill · Human choice · Kasb · Acquisition
s.422e232449550136: Inspiration placed in a heart, which may be true but is not revelation and is not proof for anyone else.
s.109a3cf85acd9b76: The Qur'an uses the word for the soul being inspired with its wrong and its right (Qur'an 91:8). Sunni scholars accept that a righteous person may be given true insight, and still refuse to build a ruling on it, because ilham is not protected from error. If an inspiration contradicts the Qur'an or the Sunnah it is set aside without argument. Sufi writing uses kashf, unveiling, for a similar idea, under the same rule.
s.daad62edfb66a1d7: Ilhaam · Elham · Elhaam · Inspiration · Divine inspiration · Kashf
s.d79d949dfc4f284f: A hidden flaw in a hadith that looks sound on the surface, found only by expert comparison.
s.22e4518d5e4e9293: A hadith carrying one is called mu'allal. The defects are subtle: a report actually stopped at a Companion but raised to the Prophet by one narrator, or two chains quietly merged into one. Detecting them took men who had memorised the variants of thousands of chains, and the great books on ilal, such as those of Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daraqutni, are among the most demanding in the field.
s.247b3c71e024f107: Illa · Ilat · Ilah · Ilal · Ilal al-hadith · Mu'allal
s.12012c9454a43c16: The biographical science of the narrators: who they were, whom they met, and how reliable each was.
s.df17edb83e2f6912: Tens of thousands of narrators were catalogued by generation, or tabaqat, so a claimed meeting between two men could be checked against their lifespans. The large references include al-Bukhari's al-Tarikh al-Kabir, Ibn Abi Hatim's al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil, and al-Mizzi's Tahdhib al-Kamal. Ibn Hajar's Taqrib al-Tahdhib condenses the verdict on each man into a line or two.
s.28467b2b0d058d65: Ilm ar-Rijal · Ilmul Rijal · Rijal · Rijaal · Ilm al-Rijaal · Asma al-Rijal
s.2264b4764e602a38: Tilting a fatha towards a kasra, so the vowel lands somewhere between an a and an e.
s.c980d1f8d497fb86: It belongs to some readings far more than others; Warsh uses a lighter form of it, called taqlil, in many places. In the Hafs reading there is one clear case, in the word majreha in Surah Hud. It is a transmitted pronunciation, not a regional accent or a matter of taste.
s.04c25aa9225a886b: Imala · Imaalah · Emalah · Imalah kubra · Taqlil · Taqleel
s.1553c088d59603a2: The person who leads the prayer, standing in front while the rows follow his movements.
s.89d6c07fa1086d4d: The word means one who is in front. The Prophet said the person who leads should be the one who knows most Qur'an, then the most learned in the sunnah. Any competent adult man can lead; it is not a clerical office or a job title, and most mosques employ one only for convenience. In wider usage imam also names a great scholar, as in Imam Malik, and in Shia Islam it carries a specific and much larger meaning.
s.ab3dbddf68cb85cd: Imaam · Emam · Imom · prayer leader · Immam · Imamah
s.5a8cfc931f36c701: The earliest of the four imams, a Kufan merchant whose school is the most widely followed today.
s.474194849ab75df2: He was born around the year 80 and died in 150, in Baghdad. He is often counted among the Tabi'un on the basis that he may have seen the Companion Anas ibn Malik as a child, though scholars discuss this. He taught by argument in a circle rather than by dictation, and his students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad ash-Shaybani wrote the school down. He refused the post of chief judge and died in prison, and he is remembered as much for that refusal as for his law.
s.03c8656a0f1964b0: Abu Hanifa · Abu Hanifah · Imam Abu Hanifa · Numan ibn Thabit · Nu'man ibn Thabit · Imam e Azam
s.ac4b4468425c8ff2: The imam of hadith who was flogged rather than say the Qur'an was created.
s.65d6b4d408cb51d6: He died in 241 in Baghdad. His Musnad gathers tens of thousands of reports arranged by the Companion who narrated them rather than by subject. Under three caliphs he was put to the test over the doctrine that the Qur'an is created, imprisoned and beaten, and refused; when the policy was finally reversed his stand was seen as having held the community's creed steady. He is reported to have forgiven the man who flogged him, and he resisted having his opinions written down as a school at all.
s.09019e4822a079ba: Ahmad ibn Hanbal · Imam Ahmad · Ahmed ibn Hanbal · Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal · Ahmad bin Hambal · Ahmed bin Hanbel
s.d336b87bb89c1479: The scholar from Bukhara who compiled the Sahih, the most rigorously sifted book of hadith.
s.6cef79af41c6a4a5: Born in 194, he lost his sight as a child and had it restored, and began memorising hadith before he was ten. He travelled for years across the Muslim world collecting reports, and required proof that a narrator had actually met the person he quoted, a stricter condition than most. Beyond the Sahih he wrote al-Adab al-Mufrad on manners and at-Tarikh al-Kabir on narrators. He died in exile near Samarqand in 256, after a dispute over a theological question.
s.8ec60900064fad0e: Imam Bukhari · Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari · Al-Bukhari · Imam Buhari · Bukhari · Imam Bukhaari
s.72fe5703074e07ed: The imam who wrote the first book on how law is derived, bridging Madinah and Iraq.
s.07fbb5b7ef152b29: Born in Gaza in 150 and died in Egypt in 204, of the Prophet's wider clan. He memorised the Muwatta and studied with Malik in Madinah, then with Abu Hanifah's student ash-Shaybani in Iraq, and so held both approaches in one head. His Risalah set out the sources of law in order and is the foundation of usul al-fiqh as a discipline. He revised his own positions after moving to Egypt, which is why the school records an old and a new opinion on some questions.
s.30578088a9af98aa: Imam Shafii · Imam Shafi'i · Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafii · Ash-Shafii · Imam Shafie · Imam Safii
s.e65a01a4ce2de882: The imam of Madinah, who taught in the Prophet's mosque and wrote the Muwatta.
s.1e462b0052ce9b9a: He died in 179 and spent almost his whole life in the city, on the reasoning that its inherited practice was itself a form of evidence. The Muwatta is among the earliest surviving books to put hadith and legal rulings side by side. He was flogged for a ruling that displeased the authorities and did not retract it. When a caliph proposed making his book the single law of the empire he refused, saying the Companions had scattered and people had learned different things.
s.302a22f7f3f26c6d: Malik ibn Anas · Imam Malik ibn Anas · Malik bin Anas · Imam Maalik · Malik · Imam-i Malik
s.e74d90d85fb17302: The compiler of the second Sahih, a student and close friend of al-Bukhari.
s.58a36a25daf6d013: He was from Nishapur and died in 261, a few years after his teacher. He held that two narrators living in the same period with the possibility of meeting is enough, without proof of an actual meeting, which is the main methodological difference between the two books. He gathered every chain of a hadith in one place instead of scattering them, which makes his book easier to study. His introduction is a short treatise on hadith criticism and is still read on its own.
s.f8e8e4c9c2b784fb: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj · Imam Muslim ibn Hajjaj · Muslim bin Hajjaj · Imam Muslim an-Nisaburi · Muslim al-Naysaburi · Imam Muslim ra
s.470fec341e3081aa: Faith: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.
s.5be24a87c48ceb49: The six articles come from the hadith of Jibril in Sahih Muslim, where the angel asks the Prophet peace be upon him what faith is and then confirms his answer. Iman is more than agreement in the mind; the texts tie it to the tongue and to the limbs as well. Most Sunni scholars hold that iman increases and decreases, while the Hanafi and Maturidi tradition holds that its essence stays fixed even as its light grows.
s.b50b9d3ef8023c20: Imaan · Eman · Emaan · Imman · Iimaan · Faith
s.2d46079bfaa50909: Turning to Allah as a settled direction of life, not only as a return after one sin.
s.0013b4e861e71b92: The Qur'an commands, turn to your Lord and submit to Him (Qur'an 39:54). Writers on the heart place inabah a step past tawbah: tawbah leaves a wrong behind, inabah keeps facing Him afterwards, in ease as well as in trouble. The picture in the root is of returning again and again to the same place.
s.a2e7c34031916f02: Inaba · Enabah · Anabah · Inabah ilallah · Munib · Muneeb
s.16d72f1385833c69: The second, shorter call given immediately before the congregation starts the prayer.
s.6684a1265dbff65c: Its words are almost those of the adhan, with the added line qad qamat as-salah, the prayer has begun. Hanafis repeat its phrases as in the adhan; the other three schools say most of them once. It is also given, quietly, by a person praying alone, and the schools differ over how binding it is.
s.5a41795673149e40: Iqama · Ikamah · Iqamat · Ikamet · Takbir of standing · second call
s.8c5767e7151f9ab1: Turning a nun sakinah or tanwin into a meem when the next letter is ba, held with a hum.
s.8af91373bc8732c9: The lips come together lightly for the meem sound and the hum is held about two counts, without pressing the lips shut. Mushafs mark it with a small meem written above the nun or the tanwin. It happens with only one letter, ba, which makes it the easiest of the four rules to spot.
s.3c10af432f862ac9: Iqlaab · Ikhlab · Eqlab · Iqlab rule · Iqlaab tajweed · converting noon to meem
s.9f7e2310a8c61eea: Submission to Allah: outwardly the five pillars, inwardly the handing over of the whole self.
s.144146d584f71a73: The word comes from a root carrying both surrender and peace, and the Qur'an calls it the religion with Allah (Qur'an 3:19). In the hadith of Jibril, islam is answered with the five pillars, iman with the six articles of belief, and ihsan with the quality of worship. So islam is the outward frame, iman the inner conviction, and ihsan the finish on both.
s.dd1559aedd58af90: Islaam · Eslam · Izlam · Submission to God · Muslim · Musulman
s.c561b3d603d09a3c: The chain of narrators who carried a hadith, listed name by name back to its source.
s.007e620df05084df: A hadith is quoted like this: so and so told me, from so and so, from so and so, that the Prophet said. Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said the isnad is part of the religion, and that without it anyone could say whatever he wished. Few traditions built a citation system this early, or held to it this stubbornly.
s.b897cdb8fe001eea: Isnaad · Esnad · Isnads · Asanid · Asaneed · Chain of narration
s.9afc2ee43e9c7446: The night the Prophet was taken to Jerusalem and then raised through the heavens.
s.ec84cda9a4b78a1f: Isra is the journey by night to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, where he led the prophets in prayer; mi'raj is the ascent from there. The Qur'an opens Surah al-Isra with the journey and Surah an-Najm describes what he saw at the Lote Tree. It was on this night that the five daily prayers were given, reduced from fifty at Musa's urging. Sunni scholars overwhelmingly hold it was in body and not only in vision, and the exact date is not established.
s.a1ee9297d8b0b5c1: Isra wal Miraj · Israa and Miraj · Miraj · Meraj · Mehraj · Lailat al-Miraj
s.2efba12a2d918bb4: Stories from earlier scriptures that entered tafsir to supply details the Qur'an deliberately leaves out.
s.b8dc650fc227c355: The Qur'an tells its stories for their lesson, so names, dates and numbers are often absent, and early commentators sometimes reached for Jewish and Christian material to fill the gaps. The rule scholars settled on has three parts: accept what our own sources confirm, reject what they contradict, and neither affirm nor deny the rest. A good deal of what people repeat as Qur'anic detail is actually israiliyyat.
s.77fc7aba2a8ad9c8: Israiliyat · Isra'iliyyat · Israeeliyyat · Isra'iliyat · Israiliyyah · Israelite reports
s.ec0b9589a5ec9c1f: Saying I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Shaytan before beginning to recite.
s.02c87b8e7b5a7204: The Qur'an instructs it directly: when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge with Allah from Shaytan the rejected. It is said once at the start of a sitting, not before every verse, and it is not itself part of the Qur'an. Most scholars treat it as strongly recommended rather than obligatory.
s.0f114efa2ac5b15c: Istiadha · Isti'aadhah · Ta'awwudh · Taawudh · Taawwuz · Auzubillah
s.e8c5981ca09101c2: Being drawn in slowly by blessings while sinning, so that ease becomes a punishment rather than approval.
s.905edb0b5d2c7b09: The Qur'an says of those who deny its signs: We will lead them on by degrees from where they do not know (Qur'an 7:182). It is the answer to a question people ask honestly, which is why the wrongdoer prospers. Comfort is not a verdict, and neither is hardship.
s.c12e6b6ff63b119d: Istidraaj · Estidraj · Istidrag · Gradual lure · Being drawn in · Respite in sin
s.f80301297af22887: Calling for help, and the disputed question of whom a Muslim may call on when it is not Allah.
s.272dd528781082ca: Everyone agrees that asking a present living person for help within their ability is ordinary and permitted, and that asking anyone at all for what only Allah can give is shirk. The dispute is narrower than it sounds: calling on an absent or deceased prophet or righteous person. Many Sufi and traditional scholars read it as a request for that person's prayer and permit it, while Hanbali and Salafi scholarship reads it as calling upon the dead and forbids it. Both sides are arguing over the meaning of one line said seventeen times a day: You alone we worship, You alone we ask for help (Qur'an 1:5).
s.55ec688c4c0be4a2: Istighatha · Istighasa · Istigatha · Isteghatha · Istighathah bil awliya · Seeking help
s.80da46453c93fd17: Asking Allah for forgiveness, usually in the words astaghfirullah.
s.a074a72e7126dacc: The Qur'an links it to relief and provision, quoting Nuh telling his people to seek forgiveness of their Lord (Qur'an 71:10). The Prophet peace be upon him, already promised forgiveness for what preceded and what would follow (Qur'an 48:2), said he sought forgiveness a hundred times a day, in Muslim. Istighfar is the request; tawbah is the turn. They are usually done together, though a person can ask for pardon before they have managed to leave the sin.
s.8a3d80ce0d52ca70: Istighfaar · Istaghfar · Estighfar · Astaghfirullah · Astagfirullah · Astaghfirullah hal azeem
s.ed0764b7396a7859: Juristic preference: setting aside a strict analogy for a stronger reason of fairness or need.
s.ca4d6081d8e38aa3: It is chiefly a Hanafi and Maliki tool, used where the obvious qiyas would cause real hardship or would collide with a text, a consensus or plain necessity. The Hanafi allowance of manufacturing contracts, where the goods do not yet exist, is a standard example. Al-Shafi'i attacked istihsan in famous words, saying whoever practises it has made law himself, though his objection was to arbitrary preference rather than to reasoned exception.
s.d2b29877e02c5db1: Istihsaan · Istehsan · Istihsen · Istihsann · Ihsan al-qiyas · juristic preference
s.1a8ee2597b14ecdf: Staying straight: keeping to the path steadily, over years, without dramatic swings.
s.11ede3c8efef6ede: When a man asked for a statement he would not need to ask anyone else about, the Prophet peace be upon him said, say I believe in Allah, then be upright, in Muslim. The Qur'an promises that angels descend on those who say our Lord is Allah and then remain steadfast (Qur'an 41:30). He also said the deeds most beloved to Allah are the most constant, even if they are few, in Bukhari and Muslim, which is the shape istiqamah usually takes in practice.
s.5718e4b8ca986f56: Istiqama · Istiqaamah · Estiqamah · Istaqim · Steadfastness · Consistency
s.3e37b6548e56eef6: Presumption of continuity: what was established stays in force until there is proof it changed.
s.80e8063acf00fa80: It is why you are still in wudu when you merely doubt whether you broke it, why a missing person is presumed alive until evidence says otherwise, and why an accused person is treated as innocent until guilt is proved. It works hand in hand with the maxim that certainty is not lifted by doubt. Shafi'is and Hanbalis use it broadly, while Hanafis accept it to defend an existing state but not to establish a new right.
s.b12f2ad2d7a13ab8: Istishaab · Istis-hab · Istishab al-hal · Istashab · presumption of continuity · presumption
s.4de896e9cb50b40f: The Qur'anic statement that Allah rose over the Throne, and the classic test case for reading divine attributes.
s.6ff16fd049c989a2: The Qur'an says the Most Merciful rose over the Throne (Qur'an 20:5). Atharis affirm the wording and leave the manner to Allah, quoting Imam Malik: the rising is known, the how is unknown, and asking about it is an innovation. Many Ash'aris and Maturidis read it as dominion and authority, to keep any bodily picture away. All three agree that Allah is not contained by a place.
s.d92f95d9547ed6ef: Istawa · Istiwaa · Istawaa · Istiwa ala al-Arsh · Rose over the Throne · Establishment on the Throne
s.d8755ae1108c00eb: Pronouncing a nun sakinah or tanwin clearly, with no nasal hum, before one of six throat letters.
s.3325f805d1ed3d57: The six are hamzah, ha, ayn, ha, ghayn and kha, all produced in the throat. Because the throat sits far from the nose, the nun is simply left as it is. There is a matching rule for a silent meem, called izhar shafawi, made at the lips.
s.211b1873553f6e7d: Izhaar · Idhar · Ith-har · Ezhar · Izhar halqi · Izhaar halqi
s.ad96ab9aa7999ef8: The Fire: the punishment prepared for those who refused, described in the Qur'an in plain and heavy terms.
s.c129fe4065160106: The Qur'an gives it names and levels and says the Fire was prepared for those who reject faith (Qur'an 2:24). Sunni belief holds that believers who enter it for their sins do not remain in it, and are brought out by mercy and intercession, while disbelief carried to the grave meets a lasting punishment. The verses are not decoration, and they are also not an invitation to guess who is going there.
s.62e4ce67344c62d1: Jahannum · Jahanam · Jahnnam · Jehennem · Dozakh · Duzakh
s.064a98aa9d7323f8: The age of ignorance in Arabia before Islam, and any conduct that still belongs to it.
s.681376112c901fdb: The root is jahl, which means recklessness and hot headed ignorance rather than illiteracy. The Arabs of that age had poetry, memory, hospitality and law, so the word is a verdict on their worship and their violence, not on their intelligence. It also names a condition rather than only a period: the Prophet told Abu Dharr, after he insulted a man over his mother, that he was a man with jahiliyyah still in him.
s.6420d9ffe2500eb1: Jahiliya · Jahilia · Jaahiliyyah · Jahiliyya · Jahalat · Age of Ignorance
s.0bda8693c1054f4d: The gathering of the Qur'an into one written volume, carried out under Abu Bakr and then Uthman.
s.e584041590881323: It was already written in the Prophet's lifetime on parchment, palm stalks and bone, and memorised by many Companions. After heavy losses among the reciters at the battle of Yamamah, Abu Bakr had Zayd ibn Thabit gather it into one set of sheets, which were later kept by Hafsah. Uthman then had standard copies made from those sheets and sent to the main cities, so that the whole community read from one text.
s.2d6d79cb91727d61: Jam al-Quran · Jamul Quran · Jam'ul Quran · compilation of the Quran · collection of the Quran · how the Quran was compiled
s.45a1ab8cd2856e86: Praying together behind one imam, which multiplies the reward of the prayer many times over.
s.a863a22d7fc97ed7: The Prophet said congregational prayer surpasses praying alone by twenty seven degrees. Two people are enough to form a jama'ah. The schools differ on how binding it is for men: Hanbalis hold it individually obligatory, Shafi'is a communal obligation, and Hanafis and Malikis a confirmed sunnah. Someone who joins late catches up alone after the imam finishes.
s.7dc226e603962148: Jamaah · Jamaat · Jama'at · Jamat · Jemaah · congregation
s.9bdc9d148ae31776: The three pillars at Mina that pilgrims pelt with small pebbles, called ramy.
s.11fa048ebd18c814: They mark the places where Ibrahim is said to have driven away the whisperer as he went to fulfil his command. On the tenth only the largest, Jamrat al-Aqabah, is stoned with seven pebbles; on the following days all three are stoned in order. The pebbles are the size of a chickpea, and the act is a symbol of refusal, not an attack on a physical devil. Those unable to go may appoint someone to stone on their behalf.
s.141529bc41fc096a: Jamaraat · Jamrah · Jamra · Jamarat bridge · Ramy · Rami al-jamarat
s.0b033c98ebd34812: A hadith book that covers every subject, not only law: belief, manners, tafsir, history and more.
s.60aadb25fc7311cb: The word means gatherer. Sahih al-Bukhari and Jami' al-Tirmidhi are both jami' works. Al-Tirmidhi's is unusual in that he comments on nearly every hadith, names who else narrated it, and records which scholars acted on it, which makes it a teaching book as much as a collection.
s.5dc204c165b84873: Jami · Jaami · Jame · Jamia · Jamiu · Jami al-Tirmidhi
s.c8aeccfeedf46dcc: The state following intercourse or sexual discharge, lifted only by a full ghusl.
s.8379ec1ff63e0cdd: A person in this state is called junub. Until they wash, prayer and tawaf are not performed and, for most scholars, the Qur'an is not recited or carried. The Qur'an mentions it plainly alongside the verse on wudu, and there is nothing shameful in it; it is simply a state with a known remedy. If water is unavailable, tayammum stands in for the ghusl.
s.37488e6bcf6a09a5: Janaba · Junub · Jinabah · Junubi · Janabat · state of janabah
s.92e691f1a4534283: Paradise: the garden of lasting delight prepared for the believers, where nothing is lost or spoiled.
s.6b62879ca0852182: The word means a garden covered over by its own foliage, and the Qur'an describes rivers, shade and gardens, then says the pleasure of Allah is greater than all of it (Qur'an 9:72). A sacred hadith describes what is in it as what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined. Firdaws is named as its highest part, beneath the Throne. In Sunni belief its greatest gift is the sight of Allah Himself.
s.0f06f1c76bde49ed: Janna · Jannat · Jennah · Cennet · Paradise · Heaven
s.e6ee251a5cfb6a5c: The main cemetery of Madinah, where much of the Prophet's family and many Companions are buried.
s.67927bdd0f97c5c3: The full name, Baqi al-Gharqad, refers to a thorn tree that once grew there. Uthman, Fatimah, Hasan ibn Ali, Aishah, Abbas and thousands of Companions lie in it. The Prophet used to visit at night and greet its people. Its graves are left level and unmarked, on his instruction that graves be kept low and not built over. The domes that later centuries raised over them were demolished in 1926, a decision Muslims still argue over, so visitors find open ground rather than monuments.
s.21173800bbc8f086: Jannatul Baqi · Baqi · Al-Baqi · Baqee · Jannat ul Baqee · Baqi al-Gharqad
s.a3ef21ea8a578fe0: The discipline of criticising or vouching for narrators, so that a chain can be judged fairly.
s.5a735661563703ef: Jarh means to wound, ta'dil to declare upright. Scholars used a graded vocabulary, from thiqah thiqah at the top down to kadhdhab at the bottom, and applied it to teachers, friends and family without flinching. The working rule is that a criticism which explains itself outweighs a general word of praise, and that a critic known for harshness is read with that in mind. This was not backbiting; it was quality control on what people were told God's Messenger said.
s.c56b8ac829830c82: Jarh wal Tadil · Al-Jarh wa al-Tadil · Jarh and Tadil · Jarh wa Taadeel · Jarh wat-Ta'deel · Jarh
s.258974c064fcf50a: A created race made from fire, unseen to us, who like people believe or disbelieve and are accountable.
s.f23f33aaa745eaa8: The Qur'an gives them a surah of their own (Qur'an 72), reports a group of them listening to the recitation and accepting it, and says they were created from a smokeless flame of fire (Qur'an 55:15). They eat, they marry, they die, and they will be judged. They are not the spirits of dead humans, and they are not behind most of what gets blamed on them.
s.d8e6736b450b6a49: Djinn · Djinns · Jinni · Jinnee · Genie · Jin
s.5ad41b95d7fc9eff: A tax historically paid by non Muslim men under Muslim rule, in place of military service.
s.cdf3b47248c22124: It is named once in the Qur'an. Classical law exempted women, children, the elderly, the poor, the disabled and monks, and the rate was scaled to ability to pay. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have granted a pension from the treasury to an elderly Jewish beggar rather than take jizyah from him. Muslims meanwhile paid zakat and were liable for military service, so the comparison was never one tax against none.
s.c51939dd8a689c83: Jizya · Jaziya · Gizya · Cizye · Jazia · Jizia
s.e342dfd63db8ae48: The Friday congregational prayer: a sermon followed by two rak'ahs, replacing Dhuhr.
s.6726bc814fcd6b53: The Qur'an commands believers to leave off trade and hurry to the remembrance of Allah when the Friday call is made. It is obligatory on adult resident men who are able to attend, and not obligatory on women, travellers or the sick, though all may attend. Whoever misses it prays Dhuhr as normal.
s.31b5f1c677c3eec0: Jumuah · Jumaa · Juma · Jummah · Jumah · Friday prayer
s.86fc6bac91457982: One of the thirty roughly equal parts the Qur'an is divided into, for reading it over a month.
s.99de21b5e08a00fb: The division is a reading aid rather than part of the revelation, and it usually cuts across a surah rather than falling neatly between two. In South Asia a juz is called a para or sipara. Reading one juz a day completes the whole Qur'an in a month, which is why almost every Ramadan schedule is built on it.
s.cc385ea4594809ae: Juzz · Juz' · Jooz · Joz · Juzu · Ajza
s.f104fd944e5e84ee: The thirtieth and last part of the Qur'an, running from Surah an-Naba to the end.
s.05ef954d7ea6ce83: It is named after its first word, amma, in the opening verse of an-Naba. It holds thirty seven short surahs, the ones most used in prayer, so it is where children and new Muslims usually begin memorising. Small printed booklets of it are sold everywhere for exactly that reason.
s.55ed7804cb29d98a: Juz' Amma · Juzu Amma · Juzamma · Amma para · Ammah · Amma Juz
s.34eda68673a33b94: The stone cube at the centre of Makkah that Muslims face in every prayer.
s.47fa9422db91d620: The name comes from a word for a cube. The Qur'an describes Ibrahim and Isma'il raising its foundations, and calls it the first house appointed for mankind. Quraysh rebuilt it during the Prophet's youth and he settled their quarrel over who would set the Black Stone by carrying it on a cloak they all lifted together. Muslims face it, they do not worship it; it is a direction, and Umar said plainly of the Black Stone that it is a stone which neither harms nor benefits.
s.768cca0dc743c3a7: Kaaba · Kaba · Kabah · Kaabah · Ka'ba · Kabe
s.fa31797d19b4997b: Major sins: the ones the texts single out with a punishment, a curse, or a warning of the Fire.
s.9ea5e8701a5bbbe6: The Qur'an promises that if you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, the smaller ones will be covered over (Qur'an 4:31). The Prophet peace be upon him named seven destructive sins in Bukhari and Muslim, among them shirk, killing a soul unjustly, and consuming interest. Scholars differ over the exact definition and therefore over the count, with classical books listing anywhere from seven to seventy and beyond. Minor sins turn serious when a person settles into them without concern.
s.459f9547b89a2059: Kabair · Kabaair · Kabirah · Kabeerah · Sagha'ir · Saghair
s.b1e309a56d8b5aef: Lying: saying what you know is not so, in speech, in a hint, or in a misleading silence.
s.b827d3e3a601223d: The Prophet peace be upon him said truthfulness leads to righteousness and lying leads to wickedness, and a man keeps lying until he is written with Allah as a liar, in Bukhari and Muslim. He named lying among the signs of hypocrisy in conduct. Scholars allow a narrow room for concealment in order to reconcile people, to protect life, and between spouses, and even there the classical preference is to use words that are true but indirect.
s.9bd4f2d2bc19c540: Kidhb · Kazib · Kizb · Kadhb · Kezb · Lying
s.a76322bbd8c56f05: A fixed expiation owed for certain deliberate breaches, heavier than simply making the act up.
s.951fc4eec6b20db4: For deliberately breaking a Ramadan fast, the expiation is to fast sixty consecutive days, or if unable, to feed sixty poor people, alongside making up the day. Hanafis and Malikis apply this to deliberate eating and drinking as well as intercourse; Shafi'is and Hanbalis restrict it to intercourse. A separate and much lighter kaffarah exists for breaking an oath. It is not owed by someone who broke the fast by mistake or out of genuine need.
s.fa9037da95d7a6ac: Kaffara · Kafara · Kaffarat · Kefaret · Kaffarah for fasting · expiation
s.fa1dcbecf3588f1a: The speech of Allah, and the classical controversy over whether the Qur'an is created or uncreated.
s.a83b51bbbf77a95d: The Qur'an is the speech of Allah, and the question the third century argued over was whether that speech is created like everything else or an eternal attribute of the One who speaks. The Mu'tazila held it created; Ahmad ibn Hanbal was imprisoned and beaten under the mihna for refusing to say so, and the position that prevailed in Sunni Islam is that the Qur'an is the uncreated speech of Allah, though the schools word the relation between the eternal attribute and the recited letters differently. It is the clearest case in the tradition of a doctrine settled by somebody's endurance rather than by an argument.
s.8ef4896320c549bd: Kalamullah · Speech of Allah · Kalam e Ilahi · Createdness of the Quran · Khalq al-Quran · Uncreated Quran
s.9970d475165bbfa7: An extraordinary event granted to a righteous believer, with no claim to prophethood attached.
s.bad884c6ab5130f0: Ahl al-Sunnah affirm karamat, pointing to Maryam finding provision out of season (Qur'an 3:37) and to the sleepers of the cave. The Mu'tazila denied them. Sunni scholars then set one plain rule: a person's uprightness on the Sunnah is the proof, not the wonder, so someone who breaks the sacred law while performing marvels is not a friend of Allah but a warning.
s.eddc78bcbb7bdfda: Karama · Karamat · Keramat · Karaamah · Kiramat · Miracle of a saint
s.588b597c8c92f4ce: The plain in Iraq where Husayn and his household were killed on the tenth of Muharram, year 61.
s.b18e19a18d2eb7c3: He had refused to pledge to Yazid and was travelling to Kufa when the army sent to intercept him cut him off from the Euphrates. Around seventy of his party were killed, including his family, and the survivors were taken to Damascus. Sunnis regard it as a grievous crime and grieve it without ritual observance, while Twelver Shia commemorate it every Muharram as a central act of devotion. Whatever a Muslim's school, the grandson of the Prophet was killed by people who called themselves Muslims.
s.3db8d7bb730c3d55: Kerbala · Karbala battle · Battle of Karbala · Kerbela · Karbalaa · Waqiat Karbala
s.35a1825e1634407c: A report; scholars use the word either as a synonym for hadith or for reports not reaching the Prophet.
s.32e97782697e0298: Three usages are recorded. Some treat khabar and hadith as the same thing. Some treat khabar as the wider word, covering reports from the Prophet and from anyone else. Some reserve hadith for the Prophet and khabar for everyone else, which is why early historians were called akhbariyyun.
s.e5f818dd0c3dc9df: Khabr · Akhbar · Akhbaar · Khaber · Kabar · Khubr
s.e179b146347e6aac: The Prophet's first wife and the first person of all to believe in him.
s.977762682803fd9a: She was a merchant of standing in Makkah who hired him for his honesty and then proposed marriage. When he came down from Hira shaking, she covered him and said Allah would never disgrace a man who carries the weak and gives to the destitute. She spent her wealth on the boycott years and died in the Year of Sorrow, before the Hijrah. All his children except Ibrahim were hers, and Jibril once sent her greetings of peace and news of a house in Paradise.
s.c657152d9a9566e3: Khadija · Khadeeja · Khadijah bint Khuwaylid · Hatice · Kadija · Khadijah al-Kubra
s.4a5f491217c44980: The commander called the Sword of Allah, who fought against the Muslims before joining them.
s.bddd9585e738c3a7: His cavalry turned the day against the Muslims at Uhud. He accepted Islam before the conquest of Makkah, saved the army at Mu'tah, and then led the campaigns against the false prophets and into Syria, where Yarmuk broke Byzantine power in the region. Umar removed him from command while he was winning, reportedly so people would learn that victory comes from Allah and not from a man. He accepted it and served under his replacement, and died in his bed in Homs.
s.aa8ceb1a6c481ce4: Khalid bin Walid · Khalid · Halid bin Velid · Khalid ibn Walid · Sayf Allah · Saifullah
s.46047d4747619ef5: Intoxicants. Wine and anything else that clouds the mind, forbidden in the Qur'an.
s.6662df2f16b4708d: The prohibition arrived in stages, ending with the command to shun it as a defilement from the work of Satan. The Prophet's rule that whatever intoxicates in large amounts is forbidden in small amounts extends the ban to every intoxicant, and it is the textbook example of qiyas at work. Hanafis kept the word khamr technically for grape wine while forbidding other intoxicants under a separate heading, arriving at the same practical result. Scholars differ over intoxicating substances used as medicine where no alternative exists.
s.24e58fa5566fcb8b: Khamar · Hamr · Khumur · Muskir · Muskirat · Nabidh
s.37392d3f29b318a9: The siege of Madinah in year five, met by digging a trench across the city's open side.
s.af62d896c28f53bc: A confederacy of Quraysh and allied tribes came to finish the matter, outnumbering the defenders several times over. Salman al-Farisi suggested the Persian tactic of a trench, which the Arabs had not seen, and the Muslims dug it in bitter cold and hunger with stones tied against their stomachs. After weeks of siege a winter wind tore the camp apart and the confederacy went home. Surah al-Ahzab is named for them and describes the fear of that month plainly.
s.1f1d2ff0826f3af6: Battle of the Trench · Ghazwat al-Khandaq · Al-Ahzab · Battle of Ahzab · Jang e Khandaq · Trench
s.03b88350fcea8016: Completing a full reading of the Qur'an from beginning to end.
s.62d7609c24425456: Many aim for one in Ramadan at a juz a day, and most mosques finish the whole text across the nights of tarawih. The Prophet told a Companion who wanted to read faster not to complete it in fewer than three days, because understanding suffers. The supplication read at the end is a widespread custom rather than a fixed text from the Sunnah.
s.eb74293eaf124514: Khatam · Khatm · Khatma · Khatmah · Khatm Quran · Khatam Quran
s.60f02f6945a4f5ab: Fear of Allah: the awareness of His justice that keeps a person from walking off the edge.
s.b43bd5c9162235b3: The Qur'an describes believers as those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned (Qur'an 8:2), and as calling on their Lord in fear and hope together (Qur'an 32:16). Scholars say the two wings must stay even: fear alone tips into despair, hope alone tips into carelessness. Healthy khawf is measured by what it makes you do, not by how bad it makes you feel.
s.2ce6518da623e1c3: Khauf · Khowf · Kawf · Khof · Khawf min Allah · Khashyah
s.2ff88e762de3b2b0: The fortified oasis north of Madinah taken in year seven, shortly after Hudaybiyah.
s.ffca15937f96e2f9: Its forts had become the base from which the confederacy against Madinah was organised. The Prophet gave the banner to Ali after saying he would give it to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger and is loved by them. After the surrender the land was left with its farmers on a share of the harvest, an arrangement later cited in the law of crop sharing. It was here that Ja'far returned from Abyssinia, and the Prophet said he did not know which gladdened him more.
s.2c2b6a01f0ecb4f7: Battle of Khaybar · Ghazwat Khaybar · Kheybar · Khaibar · Hayber · Khyber
s.90071c57d74926a1: Succession to the Prophet in governing the community, not in prophethood, which ended with him.
s.3cf66f8d12fc8c67: The word means to come after someone and stand where they stood. The office ran through the Rashidun, the Umayyads, the Abbasids and finally the Ottoman claim, and was formally abolished in 1924. Worth knowing: when the Qur'an calls Adam a khalifah, and Dawud a khalifah on the earth, it means a steward answerable for what he is given, not the political office that later took the name.
s.c10871918747fd33: Caliphate · Khilafa · Khilafat · Kalifate · Khaleefah · Khalifah
s.42fa1d38e073b81e: Divorce sought by the wife, usually by returning the mahr in exchange for her release.
s.a10fcfec4afe9fbe: Its basis is the Qur'anic statement that there is no blame on either of them in what she gives to be free, and the case of the wife of Thabit ibn Qays, who returned the garden he had given her. Scholars differ over whether the husband must agree or a judge may impose it, and over whether khul' counts as an irrevocable divorce or as an annulment, which changes the waiting period that follows. She does not need to prove wrongdoing to ask for it.
s.79f1033a5dc4bc44: Khula · Khul · Khulah · Khulaa · Khool · Hul
s.898ce7f4a09ebbf2: The four caliphs after the Prophet: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali.
s.5d09047e61329f1c: Rashid means guided along a straight road. Their rule ran from the Prophet's death in the eleventh year of the Hijrah to the killing of Ali in the fortieth, close to thirty years. The Prophet told his community to hold to his sunnah and the sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after him, which is why their practice carries a weight no later ruler's has. The title is Sunni usage; Shia hold that the succession belonged to Ali from the start. Some scholars add the six months of Hasan ibn Ali to complete the thirty years.
s.de4f3fe4d05cff06: Khulafa ar-Rashidun · Khulafa e Rashideen · Khulafaur Rashidin · Rashidun · Rightly Guided Caliphs · Four Caliphs
s.6e7128cf6dba8345: A fifth of certain wealth; in Sunni law on spoils and treasure, in Shia practice a yearly payment.
s.4c63bfd49a5e6d0e: The Qur'an assigns a fifth of the spoils of war to named recipients, and Sunni schools extend this to rikaz, wealth found buried in the ground. Twelver Shia jurisprudence reads the verse far more broadly, as a fifth of a person's yearly surplus income, paid through a marja' and divided between the share of the Imam and the descendants of the Prophet. A reader meeting the word in a Shia context is meeting this second meaning.
s.a8cff39f91beff79: Khoms · Kums · Khumus · one fifth · Khums payment · Sahm al-imam
s.f58a010bfa25300d: Stillness of the body and attention of the heart during prayer.
s.6075029d67f1cacf: The Qur'an opens its description of successful believers with those who have khushu' in their prayer. It is not an emotion you must manufacture; it is mainly the practice of returning your attention each time it wanders, and of not fidgeting. Losing focus does not invalidate the prayer, which is why nobody should stop praying out of a feeling that their prayer is not good enough.
s.9ef474b37a47dbe5: Khushu · Khushoo · Khusu · Khushuu · Kushu · concentration in prayer
s.d204af75c03fa49b: The heart's stillness and lowering before Allah, of which focus in prayer is one part.
s.f7553942c3a12b0c: The Qur'an asks whether the time has not come for the hearts of the believers to soften at the remembrance of Allah (Qur'an 57:16), which is khushu' outside the prayer as well as inside it. It is closer to a lowering than to an emotion: the heart stops standing up straight in front of its Lord. For khushu' specifically during salah, see the separate entry under worship.
s.a02d568d1da3e35f: Khushu · Khushoo · Khushu' · Khusu · Khushuu · Kushu
s.cc37bc156c972eaf: The sermon given before the Friday prayer and after the two Eid prayers.
s.4960690054684286: The Friday khutbah comes in two parts with a brief sitting between them, and it is delivered before the prayer, not after. Scholars explain it as standing in place of two of the four Dhuhr rak'ahs, so listening to it is part of the worship, and most hold that talking while it is delivered is forbidden. The Eid khutbah works the other way round: it follows the prayer, and staying for it is recommended rather than required.
s.841e6604eb019696: Khutba · Kutbah · Khudbah · Hutbe · Friday sermon · Jumuah sermon
s.2e972ab9538ceaa3: The sermon given at Arafah during the Farewell Pilgrimage, months before the Prophet died.
s.01fef81bc074fc01: The reports of it are scattered across several narrations rather than one continuous text, and popular printed versions blend them. What is firmly established: he declared blood, property and honour sacred among Muslims as sacred as that day and that place; he cancelled the interest and blood feuds of jahiliyyah, beginning with his own family's claims; he charged the men to fear Allah regarding women; and he said he was leaving them what they would not go astray by holding to. He asked them three times whether he had delivered the message.
s.cd4671a1ca9c9cfb: Farewell Sermon · Last Sermon · Khutba tul Wida · Khutbat ul Wada · Farewell Khutbah · Veda Hutbesi
s.4964b5de22b5e250: Arrogance: rejecting the truth when you hear it, and looking down on people.
s.29784e3fcc8066a5: That is the Prophet's own definition, peace be upon him, given in Muslim when a man asked whether liking good clothes counted as arrogance. He answered that Allah is beautiful and loves beauty, then gave the two signs. The Qur'an warns against walking the earth in self-importance (Qur'an 31:18). Kibr is measured by what you do with a correction, not by what you wear.
s.fb730b812ea4bc2f: Kibar · Kibir · Takabbur · Kibriya · Mutakabbir · Arrogance
s.fef8187d65af495b: The two honourable scribes who record what every person says and does.
s.86333b8b1215bb15: The Qur'an says over you are keepers, noble writers, who know what you do (Qur'an 82:10-12), and that not a word is uttered without a watcher ready beside him (Qur'an 50:18). The names Raqib and Atid come from reading two words of that verse as names rather than as descriptions. What they write becomes the record handed to each person on the Day of Judgement, a book that leaves out nothing small or large (Qur'an 18:49). The verses were given to produce attention rather than dread.
s.37671f529f966f20: Kiraman Katibeen · Kiraaman Katibeen · Recording angels · Guardian angels · Honourable scribes · Angels on the shoulders
s.ea060fcf6ab3d561: Disbelief: rejecting or refusing what a person knows Allah has revealed.
s.2a1dac87433bf9bd: The root means to cover, the way a farmer covers a seed with soil, so kufr is covering a truth that has already reached you. Scholars separate major kufr, which places someone outside Islam, from the lesser kufr that some texts use for serious sins committed by a believer. Deciding that a particular person is a disbeliever is a scholarly and judicial matter, not a conversational one.
s.2968b44f75d371f1: Kufur · Kofr · Kufer · Kafir · Kaffir · Kuffar
s.4906690382cc8255: Something vast that extends over the heavens and the earth, which most scholars hold is distinct from the Throne.
s.6cc61a30d7648f36: The Qur'an says His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and preserving them does not tire Him (Qur'an 2:255). Ibn Abbas is reported to have explained it as the place of the two feet, while others read it as His knowledge or His dominion. A narration compares the seven heavens beside the Kursi to a ring thrown into open desert, and the Kursi beside the Throne in the same way.
s.cf7d49f7ac1b08fd: Kursee · Kursiyy · Al-Kursi · Footstool · The Chair · Kursi of Allah
s.6a9a07730ee6624d: The scriptures Allah revealed, belief in them being one of the six articles of faith.
s.f297f009b034b33b: A Muslim believes that Allah spoke to earlier communities and that those revelations were true when they were given (Qur'an 2:285). The Qur'an names the Tawrat given to Musa, the Zabur to Dawud, the Injil to Isa, and pages given to Ibrahim and Musa. The mainstream position is that earlier scriptures were altered in wording or in handling over time, so present copies are not taken as authority, while the Qur'an is held to be the final one and preserved.
s.7f4c280d7018dca3: Revealed books · Books of Allah · Kitab · Kutub as-Samawiyyah · Scriptures · Heavenly books
s.f9c6d9eae8e87d00: The six hadith collections that became the standard reference set in Sunni Islam.
s.0aae032d03cee7f3: They are Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawud, Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Sunan al-Nasa'i and Sunan Ibn Majah. The list settled slowly, and some earlier scholars put Malik's Muwatta or al-Darimi's Sunan in the sixth place instead of Ibn Majah. Being in these books is not itself a grade: only the two Sahihs claim soundness throughout, while the four Sunan contain weak material their authors often flagged.
s.2787fb13fd287f19: Kutub al-Sittah · Kutub as-Sittah · Al-Kutub al-Sittah · Kutubus Sittah · Sihah Sittah · Sihah al-Sittah
s.04828f48cdc7cc8a: A verdict meaning the saying has no chain at all, so it cannot even be graded.
s.e75eeeec075c3086: This is stronger than calling something weak. A weak hadith has a chain that fails; a saying with no basis was never transmitted in the first place. Such sayings are usually folk wisdom, or a scholar's own phrase that drifted into quotation marks. A great deal of what circulates as hadith online belongs here.
s.a7d71c2ec5842408: La asl lahu · Laa asla lahu · La aslun lahu · La asla lah · No basis · No isnad
s.11d055325e54cbe0: A mistake in recitation: the clear kind changes letters or vowels, the hidden kind breaks finer rules.
s.e0fc1728b1ec3d92: Lahn jali means mispronouncing a letter or a case ending, and because it can change the meaning, scholars treat correcting it as an obligation. Lahn khafi means shortening a madd, missing a ghunnah and the like, a matter of polish rather than sin. Everyone makes both while learning; the remedy is to recite to someone who can hear them.
s.e1c95bdddb0a38e3: Lahan · Lehn · Lahn jali · Lahn khafi · Lahne jali · Lahne khafi
s.f7a3ee4e5f3f3468: The Preserved Tablet, in which everything decreed was written down before it happened.
s.6f9f424c523bb2da: The Qur'an closes Surah al-Buruj by calling it a glorious Qur'an in a Preserved Tablet (Qur'an 85:21-22), and speaks elsewhere of the Mother of the Book (Qur'an 43:4). It is the writing stage of the decree: what is in it does not change, and what a person can still change is himself. Its reality belongs to the unseen, so speculation about its material or its size is empty.
s.2e94dae4032bab4e: Lawh al-Mahfuz · Lauh Mahfooz · Loh e Mahfooz · Loh Mehfooz · Lawhul Mahfuz · Preserved Tablet
s.7d778d55d0f23943: The night in Ramadan that the Qur'an calls better than a thousand months.
s.08521b496cd8c883: A whole surah is named for it, and it says worship in that one night is better than a thousand months, which is more than eighty years. It is sought in the last ten nights of Ramadan, and most strongly in the odd ones, with the twenty seventh most commonly named; the Prophet peace be upon him said to seek it rather than announced it, and the scholars read that hiding as mercy, so that the whole ten are revived. The du'a taught for it asks Allah, who loves to pardon, for pardon.
s.feb08a5afa7723e8: Lailatul Qadr · Laylatul Qadr · Lailat ul Qadr · Shab e Qadr · Night of Power · Night of Decree
s.87d833ee52097e10: A verse or surah revealed after the migration to Madinah, whatever place it came down in.
s.0d44ad898d7a9473: Madani passages generally deal with the shape of a community: law, family, treaties, warfare, hypocrisy and the People of the Book, and they often open with O you who believe. Their verses are usually longer. Around twenty eight surahs are classed as Madani, and for a few the classification is contested or mixed.
s.1b750e33a2b44a59: Madaniyah · Madaniyyah · Madaniya · Madanee · Medinan · Medinian
s.9bd920f9e7b7db73: Lengthening a vowel with alif, waw or ya, held for a set number of counts.
s.be63004020ecc74e: The natural madd is two counts and needs no sign in the text. Longer types are triggered by a hamzah or a sukun after the vowel and stretch to four, five or six counts depending on the type and the reading. Getting the count wrong can change a word entirely, which is why madd is drilled so hard.
s.c1d32639a4f57123: Mad · Mudd · Maddah · Madd rules · Madd tabi'i · Madd asli
s.57e93f9df280ae6f: A school of law: a settled method of deriving rulings, carried by generations of scholars.
s.7a0a802a99c62b7c: The plural is madhahib, and the word means a way gone along. Four Sunni schools survive with a living scholarly tradition: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali. They agree on the pillars and on the great majority of rulings, and differ mostly in method and in detail. A madhhab is not a sect, and a Hanafi and a Shafi'i pray behind one another without difficulty.
s.e0b68359c72ccbe3: Mazhab · Madhab · Mathhab · Maslak · Mezhep · Madhhabs
s.1cfe4480d846f46e: The oasis city that took the Prophet in, where he governed, died and is buried.
s.398bdbe1a5d4e533: It was called Yathrib before he came; Madinat an-Nabi, the city of the Prophet, shortened to al-Madinah, the City. Its two Arab tribes, Aws and Khazraj, had been at war for generations and were reconciled by Islam. He declared it a sanctuary as Ibrahim had declared Makkah one, prayed for its measures to be blessed, and said that its hardship sifts people the way a furnace clears iron of impurity.
s.2fad1afa9477e9bc: Medina · Madina · Medinah · Yathrib · Madinah al-Munawwarah · Madinat an-Nabi
s.a3b12e95447b428b: Love of Allah, measured less by what it feels like and more by what it follows.
s.8b7912324bd544f0: The Qur'an says those who believe are strongest in love of Allah (Qur'an 2:165), and gives the test plainly: if you love Allah, follow the Messenger, and Allah will love you (Qur'an 3:31). Its signs are usually listed as preferring what He loves over what you want, ease in remembering Him, and love for the people who love Him. Sufi writers dwell on this station at length, but it is not a Sufi invention. It is in the verse.
s.7e48febca1ee8c5e: Mahabba · Muhabbah · Mohabbat · Mahabbat · Hubb · Hubb Allah
s.3303b195975d4a5f: A rightly guided leader expected near the end of time, understood very differently by Sunni and Shia Islam.
s.fbd77e16fca8d348: In Sunni Islam he is a future man from the family of the Prophet peace be upon him who will rule with justice, described in reports collected by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others; most scholars accepted them, while a minority, including Ibn Khaldun, criticised their chains. He is not named in the Qur'an. Twelver Shia belief is different in kind: the Mahdi there is the twelfth Imam, already born, alive in occultation, and awaited. Claimants have appeared in almost every century, and each one so far has been mistaken.
s.9a3a1c3ddd52be8b: Mehdi · Mahdee · Mehdy · Al-Mahdi · Imam Mahdi · Imam al-Mahdi
s.810d623fcde13d4d: The gift of money or property the groom owes the bride, which belongs to her alone.
s.72d0c9259e724957: The Qur'an tells men to give it graciously, as a free gift. It is not a bride price paid to her family, and nobody else has any claim on it. It may be paid at once or deferred, and there is no fixed amount: the Prophet told one man to look for even an iron ring, and in the end married him to her for the Qur'an he had memorised, while extravagance was discouraged. If a marriage ends before consummation, half is normally due.
s.988d54a2718a15c0: Mehr · Meher · Maher · Mahar · Mehir · Sadaq
s.0e8dd9cbb1ff5efd: A relative you may never marry, and before whom the rules of covering are relaxed.
s.167083fc2e31444a: The Qur'an lists them: parents, children, siblings, aunts and uncles, nieces and nephews, along with relations formed by marriage such as a mother in law, and milk relations formed by nursing in infancy. The familiar phrase about travelling with a mahram refers to this same category, together with the husband. A cousin is not a mahram, which surprises many people, and neither is a brother in law.
s.b0808c8c8b9a100e: Mehram · Muhram · Maharim · Mahrem · Mahram relative · Na mahram
s.d2fc1816f423f36c: The things forbidden while in ihram, such as perfume, cutting hair or nails, hunting and intimacy.
s.d463eff7ae883651: The Qur'an forbids sexual relations, wrongdoing and arguing during hajj, and forbids hunting land game while in ihram. To these are added perfume, cutting hair or nails, and for men sewn clothing and covering the head; most schools add contracting a marriage, which Hanafis permit. Breaking one out of forgetfulness is not sinful, though the schools differ over whether compensation is still owed, and doing it deliberately usually carries a dam or a fidyah of fasting, feeding or a sacrifice.
s.93e06cbef6a55a78: Mahzurat · Mahdhurat al-ihram · Muharramat al-ihram · ihram prohibitions · what breaks ihram · ihram restrictions
s.da82e63111c7640b: An unknown narrator, whose identity or whose reliability the scholars could not establish.
s.aa154f90cd8c4612: Two kinds are distinguished. Majhul al-ayn is a man nobody names except a single student, so we do not really know who he is. Majhul al-hal, also called mastur, is a man we can identify but whose reliability nobody recorded. A chain containing either is weak, since a report is worth only what its weakest link is worth.
s.eff504271aec0f31: Majhool · Mejhul · Majhoul · Majhool al-hal · Majhul al-ayn · Mastur
s.00921012b24b0cc8: The points in the mouth, throat and nose where each Arabic letter is produced.
s.f417c06f4335f15d: Getting these right is what keeps letters apart, so that one throat letter does not slide into another, or sin into thaa. The most common count is seventeen points, grouped in the open air of the mouth, the throat, the tongue, the lips and the nose, though some early scholars counted sixteen or fourteen. They are learned out loud with a teacher, not from a diagram.
s.498f87141e7060c6: Makhraj · Makharij · Makhaarij · Makhrij · Makhraj al huruf · articulation points
s.224e88a34c304191: The valley city holding the Ka'bah, where the Prophet was born and revelation began.
s.f25890c20450c74c: The Qur'an also calls it Bakkah, and Umm al-Qura, the mother of settlements. Ibrahim left Hajar and Isma'il in it when it had no water and no people, and prayed that hearts would incline towards it. It is a haram, a sanctuary in which fighting, hunting and cutting the trees are forbidden. Most schools bar non Muslims from its precinct, the Hanafis being the exception, and the law in force there keeps them out of the city altogether. The Prophet lived there fifty three years before the Hijrah.
s.c62f55074014b20d: Mecca · Makka · Mekka · Makkah al-Mukarramah · Bakkah · Umm al-Qura
s.05a39f011140e7ff: A verse or surah revealed before the migration to Madinah, whatever place it came down in.
s.88b2c9683838da96: The usual definition is by time rather than geography, so a verse revealed at Makkah during the farewell pilgrimage still counts as Madani. Makki passages tend to be shorter and more urgent, dealing with belief, resurrection and the earlier prophets, and often open with O mankind. Around eighty six surahs are classed as Makki, with several disputed.
s.aa66a2445b9a1a9e: Makkiyah · Makkiyyah · Makkiya · Makkee · Makkan · Meccan
s.a8239e2e73f0e610: Disliked but not forbidden: leaving it is rewarded, doing it brings no sin.
s.52db2afe17d0ce30: Wasting water in wudu, and eating raw garlic before going to the mosque, are standard examples. Hanafis split the category in two: makruh tahriman, close to forbidden and sinful to do, and makruh tanzihan, merely unbecoming. The other three schools work with a single category. So a Hanafi and a Shafi'i can use the same word and mean noticeably different things, which is worth checking before you take offence or comfort.
s.877e7c52bea288f0: Makrooh · Mekruh · Makruuh · Makrouh · Makruh tahrimi · Makruh tanzihi
s.b320d13e304856a8: Angels: beings created from light who never disobey Allah and carry out exactly what they are commanded.
s.b21f57dc9a93737a: Belief in them is one of the six articles of faith. Their creation from light is reported in Sahih Muslim rather than in the Qur'an. They are not male or female in the human sense, they do not eat or tire, and the Qur'an says they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are told (Qur'an 66:6). A few are named in the texts, most are not, and their number is known to Allah alone.
s.971e6ee0eb4fb0ae: Malaika · Malaikat · Malaaikah · Malak · Malaaika · Angels
s.c93ca86e462b7c58: The angel of death, who takes each soul at its appointed time by Allah's command.
s.0b235a7580b0255b: The Qur'an says: the angel of death, who has been put in charge of you, will take you, then to your Lord you will be returned (Qur'an 32:11). The name Izra'il is widely used but does not come from the Qur'an or from an authentic hadith, where he is simply called the angel of death. Narrations describe helpers who assist him in taking souls.
s.081af1018202600b: Angel of Death · Malakul Mawt · Malak ul Maut · Malakal Mawt · Izrail · Izra'il
s.46116ca20d60b7b8: The school of Malik ibn Anas of Madinah, weighted towards the practice of that city.
s.4f16d89122ae13af: Malik died in 179 AH, and his Muwatta is among the earliest surviving books of hadith and law together. The school prevails across North and West Africa and parts of the Gulf. It gives particular weight to 'amal ahl al-Madinah, the living practice of the people of Madinah, on the reasoning that a whole city's inherited habit is itself evidence, and it makes heavy use of maslahah and of blocking the means.
s.a122628360127a85: Malikee · Maleki · Malikiyyah · Imam Malik · Malik ibn Anas · Maliki madhhab
s.2a269a6e34a39300: The technical term in legal theory for a recommended act: the same idea as mustahabb.
s.e4a60a9f1da88c0d: Literally, something invited or called to. Legal theorists prefer mandub, while practical books of fiqh usually say mustahabb or simply sunnah. Hanafis grade the recommended further, into sunnah mu'akkadah, which the Prophet kept up consistently, and mustahabb or nafl, which he did from time to time. On that grading, habitually dropping a sunnah mu'akkadah is blameworthy, though it is not sin in the way abandoning a fard is.
s.89af859d7a4dafbf: Mandoob · Manduub · Mendub · Mandub ilayh · recommended · commendable
s.6ba1fcf82e1fb2d6: One of seven divisions of the Qur'an, used by those who complete a full reading each week.
s.b2bc4ad68a4e953c: Companions are reported to have divided their reading this way, in portions of three, five, seven, nine, eleven and thirteen surahs, with the remainder of the mushaf as the seventh. It is an older habit than the thirty part division and is still followed by some. A separate booklet of protective verses is also called Manzil; it borrowed the name but is a different thing.
s.f183fa660204eea8: Manazil · Manzeel · seven manzils · Manzil Quran · weekly division · Manzil dua
s.8953b9c51abe0227: A station on the spiritual path, in the vocabulary used mainly by Sufi writers.
s.af193055c6d0482b: In that literature a maqam is a stage the traveller reaches and holds by effort, such as repentance, patience or reliance, while a hal is a state that comes over the heart and passes, such as a moment of intense longing. The lists and their order differ from author to author. Outside Sufi writing the same qualities are discussed without this ranking.
s.8a750fff772459b9: Maqamat · Maqaam · Makam · Station · Stations · Hal
s.fc4565fa610a84cc: The stone Ibrahim stood on while building the Ka'bah, now under glass beside it.
s.d7099716f641d514: The Qur'an commands that the station of Ibrahim be taken as a place of prayer, and pilgrims pray two units behind it after tawaf. The marks on the stone are traditionally described as the impressions of his feet. It is a landmark and a reminder, not a relic with power: it is not touched, kissed or wiped for blessing, and the two units are prayed towards the Ka'bah, not towards the stone.
s.0853c45b26592205: Maqam e Ibrahim · Makam Ibrahim · Station of Abraham · Maqaam Ibrahim · Makam-i Ibrahim · Maqam Ibraheem
s.d62739fc6bf5ca46: The higher aims of Islamic law: what its rulings exist in order to protect.
s.08b5fd6470733326: Al-Ghazali and later al-Shatibi set out five: religion, life, intellect, lineage and property, with dignity and sometimes freedom added by later scholars. Interests are ranked as necessities, needs and refinements, so what preserves life outweighs what merely makes life more comfortable. Maqasid explain why a ruling exists and help reasoning where the texts are silent, but most scholars insist they cannot be used to set a clear text aside.
s.e0aa18f6427be23c: Maqasid · Maqasid al-sharia · Maqasid ash-shariah · Makasid · Maqasid shariah · Maqsad
s.06cbe46a9998c55c: A hadith in which something has been switched, such as two narrators' names or two halves of a sentence.
s.3cbdffd8e0577786: The word means turned over. Sometimes the swap is an honest slip; sometimes it was deliberate, done to test a scholar's memory or to make a chain look more impressive. A well known account describes the scholars of Baghdad testing al-Bukhari with deliberately switched chains, and his returning each text to the chain it belonged to.
s.f65b83b2acae1a44: Maqloob · Maklub · Makloob · Qalb · Maqlub hadith · Maqloob hadeeth
s.4d287e83cb4bcce9: A statement belonging to a Tabi'i, one of the generation after the Companions, traced no further back.
s.16c9348ce7cb10b2: Maqtu' and munqati' look alike and mean different things. Maqtu' is about whose saying it is; munqati' is about a hole in the chain. Much early tafsir and early fiqh is maqtu' material, valuable for understanding but not evidence from the Prophet.
s.3399c82be035d931: Maqtu · Maqtoo · Maktu · Maqtoo hadeeth · Maqtu hadith · Severed report
s.b20d5105b41a43cf: A report attributed to the Prophet himself, whether or not the chain reaching him is complete.
s.1bb5f88c728c8e52: Marfu' means raised. It describes where a report ends up, not how strong it is, so a marfu' hadith may be sahih or weak. It is contrasted with mawquf, which stops at a Companion, and maqtu', which stops at a follower.
s.8a90bdb3b1573c59: Marfu · Marfoo · Marfooa · Merfu · Marfu hadith · Marfoo hadeeth
s.71077d079aa9d5e1: Wiping over footwear in wudu instead of washing the feet, once they were put on in purity.
s.d402047eb7047df0: The permission is very widely reported from the Prophet. It lasts one day and night for a resident and three days and nights for a traveller, counted from the first wipe after wudu was broken. It ends with ghusl or with taking the socks off. Whether ordinary cotton socks qualify or only thick leather ones is an old and continuing discussion among scholars.
s.132682a903041623: Masah · Mash ala al-khuffayn · Masah on socks · wiping over socks · wiping over leather socks · Mesh ala khuffain
s.777271f44cb7afce: A hadith carried by three or more narrators at each stage, well known but short of mutawatir.
s.5914164fd4e53b75: The word simply means famous, and there is a trap in it. People also say mashhur for a saying famous on everybody's tongue, and many of those have weak chains or none at all. Fame among the public and fame in the chains are two different things.
s.2029561e2966a8c0: Mashoor · Mashhoor · Meshhur · Mashhour · Mustafid · Mustafeed
s.3e774c8bac2ed7a1: The mosque enclosure in Jerusalem, third of the three mosques worth travelling to visit.
s.abc98e786cc0b336: Aqsa means farthest, because it was the far end of the night journey from Makkah. It was the first qiblah, faced for roughly sixteen months before the direction turned to the Ka'bah. Common confusion worth clearing: al-Masjid al-Aqsa is the whole walled enclosure, including the golden Dome of the Rock and the silver domed prayer hall, not only the building people usually photograph.
s.8d0c8649e25b1c23: Al-Aqsa · Masjid ul Aqsa · Al Aqsa Mosque · Aqsa · Bayt al-Maqdis · Baitul Maqdis
s.1658a83f7adf9389: The Sacred Mosque in Makkah, the enclosure built around the Ka'bah.
s.b1ad4249a997d08f: Haram here means set apart and protected, not forbidden in the sense of sinful. It is the oldest of the three mosques a Muslim may set out on a journey to visit, and the Qur'an makes it the direction of prayer for everyone, wherever they are. A prayer offered in it is reported to be worth many times a prayer elsewhere. The open marble floor around the Ka'bah, where tawaf is made, is called the mataf.
s.98f3df7160af67df: Masjid al Haram · Masjidil Haram · Al-Masjid al-Haram · Haram Sharif · Masjid ul Haram · Grand Mosque
s.24595123517114a1: The Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, which he built himself and where he is buried.
s.a6e2f5a432f20bea: The first thing he did on arriving was buy the land and build it, with palm trunk pillars and a roof of fronds, and the poor Companions who had no home slept along its back wall. His own rooms opened onto it, and he was buried in Aishah's room, which later expansions brought inside the walls, under what is now the green dome. He said a prayer in it is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except in the Sacred Mosque.
s.edae68d86a1d914a: Masjid Nabawi · Masjid al-Nabawi · Prophet's Mosque · Masjid e Nabawi · Mescid-i Nebevi · Masjid an Nabi
s.1a61710986a9b6df: Public benefit, weighed as a legal consideration where no specific text settles the matter.
s.584088cbf3771545: Its full name is al-maslahah al-mursalah, the untethered benefit, meaning one that revelation neither commands nor forbids by name. Registering marriages, compiling the Qur'an into one volume and building prisons were all defended this way. The schools differ over how far it may reach: Malikis and Hanbalis use it most freely, Shafi'is more narrowly, and all of them insist it can never overturn a clear text.
s.01e8cedc8e5930d6: Maslaha · Masalih · Maslahat · Maslahah mursalah · Masalih mursalah · Istislah
s.451234245bba9b76: Jinn touch: the claim that a jinn can affect, or enter, a human being.
s.335bfadcb7e60eae: The Qur'an describes a man rising as one struck by the touch of Shaytan (Qur'an 2:275), and the majority of Sunni scholars, Ibn Taymiyyah among them, took the possibility as established, while a minority read the verse as an image rather than a report. Even among those who affirm it, the classical books warn that most cases brought to them turned out to be illness, hardship or imagination. Where the symptoms are physical or psychiatric, the ordinary duty to seek medical treatment is not suspended.
s.8bd2b717687f0a55: Mass · Al-mass · Mas · Sar · Sara' · Possession
s.3c4e781394f785ed: The actual wording of a hadith, the part that comes after the chain of narrators.
s.46be8c7469c85976: The word means the firm surface of the ground, or the back of something. Scholars weigh the matn as well as the chain. A text that contradicts the Qur'an, or a plain fact, or promises an enormous reward for a tiny act, is treated with suspicion even when the chain looks tidy.
s.58a6cd09398b8493: Matan · Matin · Mutun · Matoon · Text of the hadith · Hadith text
s.b6cfa7c70c973bf1: A report from a narrator the scholars abandoned, usually one accused of lying or of gross error.
s.66bb5d6e679de094: Matruk sits just above fabricated. It is described as severely weak, da'if jiddan, and unlike ordinary weakness it cannot be repaired by supporting chains. When a book says a narrator is matruk al-hadith, the discussion is effectively over.
s.2fb226cd7a7e3db3: Matrook · Metruk · Matrook al-hadith · Matruk al-hadith · Abandoned narrator · Daif jiddan
s.2bc14de685be0248: A Sunni school of creed founded by Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, closely tied to the Hanafi tradition.
s.0e30a011fea35dd3: It grew in Samarqand and became the creed of most Hanafis, and so of much of Turkey, Central Asia, and the Indian subcontinent. It stands close to the Ash'ari school and differs on a set of fine points, such as how far reason alone can establish that Allah must be known before revelation arrives, and whether iman itself increases and decreases. Each school counts the other as Sunni.
s.f947eb95d1805293: Maturidiyyah · Maturidiyya · Matureedi · Maturidee · Maturidis · Abu Mansur al-Maturidi
s.aead99cca2bef9e6: A fabricated report, invented and then attached to the Prophet; not really a hadith at all.
s.a12da444019d4362: The word means placed, or set down, as in something put there by a human hand. Fabrications were made for many motives: sectarian argument, storytelling, flattery of rulers, and misplaced zeal for encouraging worship. The Prophet's warning against deliberately lying about him is among the most widely transmitted reports in existence. Scholars wrote whole books listing fabrications so people could recognise them.
s.83fadf86164c4440: Mawdu · Mawdoo · Maudu · Maudhu · Mawzu · Mauzoo
s.e5680e4506f7a95f: A report that stops at a Companion: his own statement or action, not attributed to the Prophet.
s.e8595a875d600865: Mawquf means halted. Such reports carry real weight, since the Companions watched the practice first hand. Some mawquf statements are treated as effectively marfu', for instance when a Companion speaks about something no one could know except through revelation.
s.59a7632766eaa149: Mawqoof · Mauquf · Maukuf · Mevkuf · Mawqoof hadith · Stopped at a Companion
s.a000a119d23d371f: The valley near Makkah where pilgrims camp before Arafah and for the days after Eid.
s.a8d869e461ad4c4a: Pilgrims stay there on the eighth of Dhul Hijjah, called the day of tarwiyah, then return on the tenth after Arafah and remain for the days of tashriq, the eleventh to the thirteenth. The three jamarat stand at its edge. A pilgrim may leave after the twelfth if they depart before sunset; otherwise the thirteenth is completed.
s.af0b97788f3e0e52: Muna · Minaa · Mena · tent city · valley of Mina · Mina tents
s.3877a03516b7e6f3: The fixed boundary points where a pilgrim must enter ihram before continuing towards Makkah.
s.0da79ced8c6cd62f: The Prophet named four, one on each approach: Dhul Hulayfah for Madinah, al-Juhfah for Syria and Egypt, Qarn al-Manazil for Najd, and Yalamlam for Yemen. Dhat Irq, for those coming from Iraq, was fixed by Umar, and some report it from the Prophet as well. Anyone travelling through one, including passengers on a flight passing over it, enters ihram there or before. There is also a miqat in time: the months of hajj, Shawwal, Dhul Qa'dah and the first days of Dhul Hijjah.
s.7eb8531b43c71955: Meeqat · Mikat · Miqaat · Mawaqit · Miqat boundary · Dhul Hulayfah
s.c959ceb61b6fd924: Islamic inheritance: fixed shares of an estate distributed among relatives named in the Qur'an.
s.b70801d178269137: It is also called 'ilm al-fara'id, the science of the fixed portions, and it is the most mathematical corner of fiqh. The order is debts first, then any bequest up to a third, then the shares. Some heirs take a stated fraction while the remainder passes to the nearest male agnate, and because the cases interlock, one heir's presence can change another's share entirely. Most families need someone who knows the subject to work an estate out correctly.
s.33c05a3f0d06e781: Meerath · Meeras · Miras · Faraid · Faraidh · Virasat
s.ad359e147152e87e: The scale on which deeds are weighed on the Day of Judgement, with exact justice.
s.2615ea227fec2b90: The Qur'an says the scales of justice will be set up for the Day of Resurrection, so that no soul is wronged in anything, even the weight of a mustard seed (Qur'an 21:47). Sunni belief takes this as a real scale and not only a figure of speech. Some small deeds are described as heavy upon it, far out of proportion to the effort they cost, which is worth remembering.
s.3343e50bc4fd6fa5: Meezan · Mizaan · Meezaan · Tarazu · Mizan al-Amal · The Balance
s.6bab0e4cfd82904a: A chain with its beginning cut off, where the author omits the narrators nearest to himself.
