The word itself is the receipt, and every lute an angel holds in a Renaissance painting began as an oud. The guitar is where we slow down: its name likely descends from the Greek kithara by a separate road, and medieval Spain knew both a guitarra latina and a guitarra morisca. Call the oud the guitar’s grandmother by marriage, and grade it traced.
s.573f2875b7b3efb3: Every lute in an old painting, and more distantly every strummed guitar, echoes the wood of al-Andalus.
s.fcc9fc1b56cb1345: A chemical reaction is over in femtoseconds, millionths of a billionth of a second, and for all of chemistry’s history the actual moment of change, bonds breaking and forming, was invisible in principle: you could know the before and the after, never the during. Ahmed Zewail, born in Damanhur, Egypt, educated in Alexandria and then in America, built the camera for it. At Caltech in the 1980s his team learned to fire laser pulses brief enough to catch molecules in mid transformation, strobe lighting the instant itself. Chemistry acquired slow motion. In 1999 the Nobel committee gave him the chemistry prize alone, an undivided honor, for founding femtochemistry.
s.51f90276fcf76724: Zewail carried the recognition home with intent. He argued tirelessly that science is the modern world’s common wealth, and that the Arab and Muslim worlds must reclaim their seat at its table not by nostalgia but by laboratories, founding a city of science outside Cairo that now bears his name. He liked to say he was formed by both the Nile and the Pacific and refused to choose between them. When he died in 2016, Egypt gave him a state funeral with full honors, a scientist mourned like a head of state. His field opened the door to attosecond physics: chemistry’s camera is still speeding up.

s.dfa72d132707cf69: Skyscrapers before Fazlur Rahman Khan were brute force: stack a dense internal skeleton and pay for it in steel, money, and darkness. Khan, an engineer from Dhaka who joined a Chicago firm, saw that a tall building could work instead like a hollow tube, its strength moved to the perimeter, walls of closely spaced columns or great visible braces carrying the wind. The idea unfolded in stages: the framed tube, then the braced tube of the John Hancock Center, then the bundled tube of the Sears Tower, nine tubes clustered like reeds, the world’s tallest building for a quarter century, raised with far less steel than the old way would have demanded.
s.07498c8990a4af1b: Khan was among the first engineers to put computers seriously to work on structures, and colleagues remembered a gentle man who quoted poetry and insisted that engineering serve people rather than ego. He kept faith with Bengal, organizing relief for Bangladesh from his Chicago living room during the 1971 war. He died at fifty two, too early to watch his ideas conquer the world’s skylines, but nearly every supertall tower since, including the Burj Khalifa, descends from his structural grammar. When a city’s glass towers catch the evening light, the quiet shape doing the work inside them is usually his.

s.ab2f604e3888b5d8: The Qur'an calls marriage a mithaq ghaliz, a heavy covenant (4:21). The same weight of phrase is used for the pact Allah took from the prophets. That is the register: not a party, not a transaction between families, but a solemn undertaking witnessed before Allah.
s.1cf33c6c7fb7a392: Because it is a covenant, it has terms, witnesses, and consequences. Islam did not romanticise marriage into vagueness; it wrote it down.
s.940551685a7a508a: Among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves so that you may find rest in them, and He placed between you love and mercy (30:21). Three words carry the verse: sukun, rest; mawadda, warm love; rahma, mercy.
s.c7587f1c2462f26a: Notice the order of the years: the love that begins a marriage is named, and so is the mercy that keeps one going long after the beginning has grown quiet.

s.35c2ef11078c71eb: Calibrate it first: open the compass app and move the phone in a wide figure of eight a few times until the app stops asking. Then stand away from steel doors, radiators, speakers, laptops and reinforced concrete columns, all of which pull the needle. Check the reading in two or three spots in the room; if they disagree, the metal is lying to you, not the sky. Many phone compasses can show true north instead of magnetic north in their settings, and that is the setting you want.

s.f89bf33ec17884b4: A shadow is an honest instrument. Two ways to use it:
s.6cd8dd424fa397cc: Find true north from the shortest shadow
s.1afedb96998549f0: Stand a straight stick upright on flat ground in the morning and mark the tip of its shadow every fifteen minutes through the middle of the day. The shortest shadow of the day is the moment of solar noon, and it lies exactly along the true north to south line: in the northern hemisphere the shadow points true north, in the southern hemisphere it points true south. Draw that line on the floor, then measure the qibla angle from it with a protractor.
s.48cdd220c26fd7b6: The two days the sun stands over the Kaaba
s.e2f188fd57096f1f: Twice a year the sun passes directly over the Kaaba, and at that instant any upright object anywhere on the sunlit half of the earth casts a shadow pointing exactly away from Makkah: face along the shadow toward the sun and you face the qibla. It happens around 27 and 28 May at about 12:18 in Makkah, which is 09:18 UTC, and around 15 and 16 July at about 12:27 in Makkah, which is 09:27 UTC. Convert those UTC times to your own clock, wait for a sunny minute, and mark the line on the floor. This check needs no compass, no phone and no trust in either.
s.d45163380ef5f3f6: This page computes the great-circle bearing, the initial heading of the shortest path over a spherical earth, from your point to the Kaaba at latitude 21.4225 north, longitude 39.8262 east. It is the calculation used by nearly every qibla instrument and by the great majority of scholars. It is why masjids in North America face east and north of east rather than south east: on a globe, the shortest way to Makkah from Ottawa crosses the north Atlantic, and a flat map lies about that.
s.f5f76d0b4db068d1: The distance shown is the great-circle distance on a sphere of mean radius 6371 kilometres, accurate to a few kilometres in several thousand.

s.f3f0773df1133e07: Before there was history there was a announcement: 'I am placing upon the earth a successor' (2:30). The angels asked about bloodshed; Allah answered with knowledge. He created Adam from clay, breathed into him of His spirit, and taught him the names of all things, a knowledge the angels themselves did not carry. When they were commanded to prostrate to him, all obeyed except Iblis, whose refusal, born of pride, opened the oldest war in creation.
s.40856ba1412ab69b: Adam lived in the Garden with his wife Hawwa, free in all of it except one tree. The whisperer swore he was a sincere adviser, and the two ate. What happened next is the heart of the human story: they did not argue, they did not blame their Lord. They said the sentence every child of theirs has needed since: 'Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves' (7:23). Adam received words from his Lord, and his Lord turned to him. He descended to the earth not as a punishment without hope but as a successor beginning his work.
s.aab79d9c55f42372: Every funeral, every repentance, every human face carries his inheritance. The Qur'an insists on the likeness: 'The example of Isa in the sight of Allah is like that of Adam: He created him from dust' (3:59). Dignity, slip, return. That is the pattern, and it began with him.

s.d9e9d556a2c39454: When idols first stood between people and their Maker, Allah sent Nuh, the first messenger to a nation. His method is described in his own words in the surah that bears his name: 'My Lord, I called my people night and day, but my calling only increased them in flight' (71:5-6). He called publicly and privately, with promises of rain and wealth and gardens if they would only seek forgiveness. For nine hundred and fifty years (29:14) the answer was fingers in ears and cloaks pulled over faces.
s.56c7366332ca2d9d: The believers were a handful, and the chiefs mocked them as 'the lowest among us'. When the decree came, Nuh was commanded to build an ark far from any sea, under their eyes and under their laughter: 'Every time chiefs of his people passed him, they ridiculed him' (11:38). Then the ovens of the earth gushed, the sky opened, and the ship carried the believers and pairs of every kind upon waves like mountains.
s.64b84f5b3c861699: The hardest verse of his story is a father's: his own son refused to board, trusting a mountain against the water of Allah. 'And the waves came between them, and he was among the drowned' (11:43). When Nuh appealed, the answer drew the line that defines faith forever: kinship is conduct, not blood. The ark settled on Judiyy, and mankind began again from the people of gratitude. The Qur'an calls him 'a grateful servant' (17:3), and every prophet after him sails in his wake.
s.4be71f205cbd6596: 'My Lord, I called my people night and day.' The patience of nine centuries in one line.
s.4ba7760956f22953: 'He remained among them a thousand years less fifty.' The longest recorded mission in the Book.
s.912e0fc2815b4918: He builds the ark on dry land while the chiefs laugh; he promises their laughter will change sides.
s.aaf5c3260fff0ff8: His son chooses a mountain over the mercy; the waves come between them.

s.8a17e99130a0b8eb: The people of 'Ad were the bodybuilders of ancient Arabia: giants of construction who raised 'Iram of the pillars, the like of which was never created in the lands' (89:7-8). Strength became their theology; 'Who is mightier than us?' they asked. To them Allah sent one of their own, Hud, with the oldest sentence of the prophets: O my people, worship Allah, you have no god other than Him.
s.9e6dca120529af08: He asked no wage, promised increase upon their strength if they sought forgiveness, and warned that towers do not negotiate with heaven. They answered with contempt. So the punishment came in the very shape of their pride: air. A wind, 'barren' (51:41), screaming cold, seven nights and eight days (69:7), that left the people like hollow palm trunks thrown down. The strongest tribe of the age was undone by something no wall can stop.
s.3321aa554428a377: Hud and the believers were saved by mercy 'from Us' (11:58). His story stands in the Qur'an as the permanent answer to every civilization that mistakes muscle for meaning.
s.85a5f2d3dd01d629: 'And to 'Ad, their brother Hud. He said: O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him.'
s.141fda27a1a34079: 'Iram of the pillars, the like of which was never created in the lands.' The peak they trusted.
s.a36cd33b0bef6829: Seven nights and eight days of the barren wind; a people left like hollow palm trunks.
s.36676416a044a720: 'And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him, by mercy from Us.'
s.40430499886de737: Thamud inherited the lesson of 'Ad and carved their security into the mountains themselves, hewing homes from living rock 'with skill' (26:149). To them came their brother Salih. They demanded a sign on their own terms, and Allah gave them one that walked and drank: a she-camel, 'the she-camel of Allah' (91:13), with a simple covenant attached. She drinks on her day, you on yours. Do not touch her with harm.
s.4fd384af3aa0e24d: It was a test of the smallest thing: restraint. The city's worst man was called for the job, and the tribe consented as he hamstrung her (91:14). The Qur'an's accounting is precise: one man cut, but 'they' killed, because approval is participation. Salih gave them three days. Then the sayhah, a single devastating cry, took them in their homes, and the carved rock kept standing over no one.
s.c3a53477877fac35: 'This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you; let her eat in Allah's earth and do not touch her with harm.'
s.d98b0955c07f083b: The messenger of Allah told them: the she-camel of Allah and her drink. Then they denied and hamstrung her.
s.97749999460c4c5f: 'And you carve out of the mountains, homes, with skill.' Security chiseled into stone.
s.9ee7bcffe25fe349: 'Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days: a promise not to be belied.'

s.62cb3ce1c0e8fc73: Khalilullah · the intimate friend · one of the five of firm resolve · The father of the prophetic line
s.869f14d2a351d7e0: Ibrahim reasoned his way out of his whole civilization while still young. He watched a star set, a moon set, a sun set, and concluded that whatever sinks cannot be a lord (6:76-79). Then he did what no polite philosopher would: he walked into his people's temple and reduced the idols to splinters, leaving the biggest one standing with the axe, so the statue could be interviewed (21:58-63). The argument won itself; their answer was a bonfire built by a whole city.
s.66b9c7cea261e428: To the fire, the Owner of fire said: 'O fire, be coolness and peace upon Ibrahim' (21:69). He walked out unburned into a life of departures: from his father who chose the idols, from his homeland, and finally into the barren valley where he left Hajar and the infant Ismail with nothing but trust and a prayer that hearts would fly toward them (14:37). Zamzam answered from under a baby's heel; a city answered over centuries.
s.e9c4621b61d0dd1d: Then the hardest test ever put in a dream: the sacrifice of the son given in old age. Father told son; son answered, 'Do as you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, of the patient' (37:102). The blade was on its way when heaven called it a fulfilled vision and sent the ransom ram. Out of that surrendered family came the House: Ibrahim and Ismail raising the foundations of the Kaaba, praying over wet stone for a messenger to rise from that valley (2:127-129). Every prayer of every Muslim ends by blessing him, the one the Qur'an calls 'an ummah in himself' (16:120) and whom Allah took 'as an intimate friend' (4:125).
s.98cac38c5a7e2b22: 'O fire, be coolness and peace upon Ibrahim.' The element obeyed its Owner.
s.50e128b6c0b183e8: Father and son at the summit of surrender: 'Do as you are commanded.'
s.5dd2ccf42ed6c74a: 'And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Ismail: our Lord, accept from us.'
s.314a8fb8e3f2e706: 'Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in a valley without cultivation, by Your sacred House.' The birth-prayer of Makkah.
s.57a533e37db2a37d: 'Ibrahim was an ummah, devoutly obedient to Allah, inclining to truth.' One man counted as a nation.
s.4d761a4272e23a50: 'And Allah took Ibrahim as an intimate friend.' Khalilullah.
s.835d9313ded9ff15: “The first of creation to be clothed on the Day of Resurrection will be Ibrahim.”

s.a0b1ac6d9efb430f: Sent to the cities of the plain · Contemporary of Ibrahim
s.7679522f56f5d6ad: Lut believed in Ibrahim when a whole empire did not, and migrated with him (29:26). He was then sent to cities whose people pioneered a transgression no nation before them had committed, and added highway robbery and open evil in their gatherings to it. Lut's position was that of every reformer alone in a hostile town: no clan to shield him, guests he could not protect, and a wife whose loyalty was with the city.
s.4f77799582dcc8e3: The crisis came disguised as hospitality. Angels in the form of handsome young men arrived at his door, and the town came running. 'This is a distressing day,' he said (11:77), offering the path of purity and being mocked for it. Then the guests unveiled: we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. Travel with your family in the night, and let none of you look back (11:81).
s.0c3730528a5dd894: At dawn the cities were lifted and overturned, and stones of layered clay rained down, 'marked in the presence of your Lord' (11:83). His wife, who chose the people over the prophet, was counted with them; the Qur'an names her with Nuh's wife as the eternal proof that nearness to a righteous man saves no one without faith of her own (66:10). The believers walked out with the dawn.
s.1ba021f173656da7: The guests arrive; Lut, unable to protect them, calls it a distressing day.
s.9dc1513150a47787: 'We are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. Set out with your family in a portion of the night.'
s.2fce82f2a7789744: The cities turned upside down, and stones of baked clay in layers.
s.92bb0b3a24a13fc8: The wives of Nuh and Lut: married to two righteous servants, yet betrayal made marriage no shelter.
s.32728b8698e71cf0: The sacrifice ransomed · Son of Ibrahim
s.2e9984eee22b6638: His life begins as the answer to a prayer for righteous offspring (37:100) and unfolds as a series of surrenders. As an infant he is left with his mother Hajar in a valley of bare rock, because Allah commanded it; her sprint between Safa and Marwa searching water for him is re-walked by every pilgrim to this day, and the spring that broke out at his feet still flows: Zamzam.
s.3f614b9f86700651: As a boy old enough to run at his father's side, he was told of the dream in which he was the offering. His answer is the calmest sentence in scripture: 'O my father, do as you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, of the patient' (37:102). The ransom came, and the surrender stayed. The Qur'an gives him a rare personal title: sadiq al-wa'd, true to the promise (19:54).
s.6a62342a45f56d24: 'O my father, do as you are commanded.' The offering agrees to the offering.
s.5ececb72e870f100: 'He was true to the promise, and was a messenger and a prophet.'

s.bcc6ead80a1aab96: The laughing promise · Son of Ibrahim
s.d50b2ce7dd7ef7a1: He was announced by angels who would not eat. When Ibrahim's mysterious guests refused the roasted calf, fear crept in; then they gave their news: a boy, from Sarah, who stood listening and laughed (11:71). She voiced the impossibility, an old woman and an old husband, and received the answer that governs the whole prophetic story: 'Do you wonder at the command of Allah?' (11:73). His very name carries the laughter of that day.
s.6aed9335909e53f3: The Qur'an calls him 'a prophet from among the righteous' (37:112) and pairs him constantly with his father and his son: Ibrahim, Ishaq, Yaqub, a chain of 'strength and vision' (38:45-47). Through his line came the long procession of Bani Israil's prophets: Yusuf, Musa, Dawud, Sulayman, down to Isa. One elderly couple's impossible child became half the chain of light.
s.9ca0a1d27eb092e0: Sarah, standing, laughs; the glad tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Yaqub.
s.a9dfde7d7404a04f: 'And We gave him good tidings of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous.'
s.f2b1e1cf611731f5: Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub: possessors of strength and vision, chosen for the remembrance of the Home.
s.daadee6e0eaebccc: “The noble, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble: Yusuf, son of Yaqub, son of Ishaq, son of Ibrahim.”
s.865acedb96442b91: Israil · father of the twelve · Grandson of Ibrahim
s.45e90ebcd77b8bae: Yaqub, also named Israil, fathered the twelve tribes and one impossible grief. He read his son Yusuf's dream correctly and warned him of brothers' envy, then lost that son to those very brothers and was handed a shirt with false blood. His response gave the ummah a phrase it has leaned on ever since: 'sabrun jamil', beautiful patience, patience with no public bitterness in it (12:18).
s.1cce56c1666b7e73: For years he wept until his eyes whitened, yet his theology never bent: 'I only complain of my anguish and grief to Allah' (12:86). Grief and faith, the Qur'an insists, can share one chest. He never stopped expecting mercy: 'Do not despair of the relief of Allah' (12:87). When Yusuf's shirt came back the second time, thrown over his face, his sight returned, and the old man who had been mocked for hoping said: did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?
s.882c1ccca7628e66: His last scene is the Qur'an's model deathbed: 'What will you worship after me?' he asked his sons, and heard the only inheritance that mattered secured: your God and the God of your fathers, one God, and to Him we surrender (2:133).
s.11a0466dda995587: Handed the false-blooded shirt: 'so patience is beautiful.' Sabrun jamil enters the language.
s.05805367eb184499: 'I only complain of my anguish and grief to Allah.' Sorrow with perfect address.
s.b323451f193217f1: 'Do not despair of the relief of Allah; none despairs of it except the disbelieving people.'
s.036f25f3cd793679: The deathbed question: 'What will you worship after me?' The answer that mattered more than any estate.
s.2bc35711dc1daf5b: Israil, father of the twelve tribes
s.bae2001871e10bb6: The most beautiful of stories · Son of Yaqub
s.abcdf2559712dc5b: The Qur'an calls his chapter 'the most beautiful of stories' (12:3) and it is the only prophet's life told whole, in order, in one surah. It opens with a boy's dream, eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrating, and a father's warning to hide it from envious brothers. The envy moved anyway: a plot, a well, a passing caravan, and the beloved son of a prophet sold for a few coins into Egypt.
s.60b084b819c16c96: Beauty became his next trial. The wife of his master locked the doors; his answer, 'I seek refuge in Allah' (12:23), cost him his freedom, because in that house truth was weaker than reputation. He chose the cell over the sin in one of scripture's most quoted prayers: 'My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to' (12:33). In prison he interpreted dreams and preached One God, and was forgotten for years by the man he helped.
s.e647e50d0b2697c7: Then Pharaoh's dream of seven lean cows unlocked everything. Yusuf would not leave the cell until his name was cleared, then asked for the hardest job in the kingdom: 'Set me over the storehouses of the land' (12:55), and steered Egypt through seven years of famine. When the brothers came begging grain from the brother they had thrown away, he watched them, tested them, and finally spoke: 'I am Yusuf.' Their terror met the sentence by which the whole surah is remembered: 'No blame upon you today; may Allah forgive you' (12:92).
s.2972cabd45c610b3: The dream closed its circle: parents and brothers prostrating, the boy from the well now the story every wronged person reads to learn how power and pardon can share one heart. His last recorded words are not about Egypt at all: 'Let me die as a Muslim, and join me with the righteous' (12:101).
s.0e79e5be67275d44: 'O my father, I saw eleven stars and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me.' The seed of the whole story.
s.7204dee46f57c73e: 'She was determined, and he would have been, had he not seen the proof of his Lord.' Honesty about temptation, and the rescue in it.
s.d92cf9c4e4fb92b2: 'My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to.' The cell chosen over the sin.
s.9b8a2c18df0888f2: 'Set me over the storehouses of the land; I am a knowing guardian.' Competence offered where it was owed.
s.6ad37c991163ecff: 'No blame upon you today.' The most powerful man in Egypt, forgiving from strength.
s.32e9c9af2658b439: 'Let me die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous.' A king's only remaining wish.

s.cb31d100acad098a: Patience under ruin · Of the line of Ibrahim
s.43d59151d0b3d26f: Ayyub had everything a man can lose: wealth, lands, children, health. Then he lost it, layer by layer, until illness sat on him for years and only his wife's loyalty remained. The whisperer waited for the complaint that never came. When Ayyub finally turned to his Lord, listen to the manners in it: 'Adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful' (21:83). No accusation, no demand, barely even a request; a description laid at the door of Mercy.
s.c25c7ad7e0eda05d: The answer restored him with interest: 'Strike the ground with your foot; here is a cool washing and a drink' (38:42). Healing rose from under his own heel, family was returned and doubled, 'a mercy from Us and a reminder for those of understanding' (38:43). Even his tender dilemma, an oath sworn in illness to discipline his wife, was solved by heaven with gentleness: take a bundle of grass and fulfill the oath's letter without its harshness (38:44).
s.e5eff2017df02307: The Qur'an closes his file with the words every sufferer hopes to earn: 'Indeed We found him patient. An excellent servant! He was ever turning back' (38:44).
s.c91c0b85b6db2bf3: 'Adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.' The politest cry in scripture.
s.484357b0627c4b62: 'Strike the ground with your foot.' Healing from under his own heel.
s.f2c20a772bcff8d5: 'Indeed We found him patient. An excellent servant, ever turning back.'
s.8d3fafe34da27b45: “While Ayyub was bathing, gold locusts fell upon him and he began gathering them in his garment. His Lord called: had I not enriched you? He said: yes my Lord, but I am never free of need for Your blessing.”
s.b8a6360766fec2cd: Preacher to the cheating scales · Before Musa
s.227c308bc05f47d1: Madyan sat on the caravan roads and grew rich the short way: shaving the measure, tipping the scales, sitting on every path to threaten and cut off travelers. To them Allah sent Shuayb, called by the scholars 'the orator of the prophets' for the beauty of his pleading. His message fused the mosque and the market: worship Allah alone, and give full measure and weight (7:85). In this religion, the scale is an altar.
s.001d2830cc1aa1de: They answered like every economy defending its sins: 'Does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we stop doing what we will with our wealth?' (11:87). His reply is a working manifesto for every honest merchant since: 'I only intend reform as much as I am able; my success is only through Allah' (11:88). He wanted no advantage over them; he would not secretly do what he forbade.
s.e7acca15d4bf06e3: The mockery hardened, the threats of exile came, and the cry seized the wrongdoers kneeling in their homes, 'as if they had never prospered there' (11:95). Trade built Madyan; fraud erased it.
s.23d0d73e55603104: 'Give full measure and weight, and do not deprive people of their due.' The market summoned to worship.
s.ba5edbde27d07b90: Their sarcasm: 'Does your prayer command you...?' Wealth claiming independence from God.
s.1bb011a69f75cbcc: 'I only intend reform as much as I am able; my success is only through Allah.' The reformer's creed.
s.fd54a32e2249f53c: Kalimullah · spoken to directly · one of the five of firm resolve · Bani Israil in Egypt
s.4d4e31ba1db52c18: No name sounds in the Qur'an more often than Musa: one hundred and thirty-six times. His story begins with an empire killing newborn boys and a mother inspired to answer terror with trust: put your baby in a chest and give him to the river (28:7). The current delivered Israel's deliverer to Pharaoh's own doorstep, and heaven arranged the nursing contract so the paid nurse was his own mother. 'And I cast love upon you from Me' (20:39).
s.aeee603e71c4fb40: Grown strong, he struck an oppressor to defend a stranger, and the man died. He fled to Madyan with nothing, watered two women's flock at a well, and prayed the migrant's masterpiece: 'My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me' (28:24). Ten years of shepherding, a wife, and then a fire on the side of a mountain that was not a fire. At Tuwa, sandals off, a voice from the tree: 'Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance' (20:14).
s.5f297795fb60e3ef: Sent to the tyrant he was raised by, he asked first for inner repair: 'My Lord, expand for me my chest, and ease for me my task, and untie the knot from my tongue' (20:25-27), and for his brother Harun as partner. The duel with Pharaoh escalated from staff-serpent to plagues to the night flight, until the sea stood in front and the army behind and his people despaired. His answer at the water's edge is the sentence of every cornered believer: 'No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me' (26:62). The sea split into walls; the pursuer drowned in the closing corridor, believing one wave too late.
s.16478ba6c3b8d938: 'We inspired the mother of Musa: nurse him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear or grieve.'
s.2f707269b8e47a93: At the fire of Tuwa: 'Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me.'
s.5135f4f993b79ea3: 'My Lord, expand for me my chest.' The prophet's request before the tyrant's court: an opened heart.
s.f214823e240adaf4: Sea ahead, army behind: 'No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me.'
s.baba4908d9b8c8c2: 'You will not see Me, but look at the mountain.' The mountain leveled; Musa fell thunderstruck.
s.c5b7538ca903108a: 'And Allah spoke to Musa with direct speech.' Kalimullah.
s.d04a9afeb38ac490: 136 times · the most of any name
s.52aeebec09a16de6: The eloquent brother · With Musa in Egypt
s.a682c160f1d715ae: Harun is the only prophet in the Qur'an who became one because another prophet asked. Standing before the mission of his life, Musa prayed: 'Appoint for me a minister from my family: Harun, my brother. Increase through him my strength' (20:29-31), praising his brother's superior eloquence (28:34). The answer, 'We will strengthen your arm through your brother' (28:35), made brotherhood itself a prophetic institution.
s.bdbd93256595de63: He stood beside Musa through every round with Pharaoh, and then faced his own crucible alone: left in charge while Musa was on Sinai, he watched the people melt their jewelry into a calf. He pleaded, warned, and was nearly killed for it (7:150); when Musa returned in fury and seized him, Harun's answer, 'O son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head' (20:94), chose the unity of the ummah over his own vindication until the matter could be judged rightly.
s.4e5cd9eabe538680: 'Appoint for me a minister from my family: Harun, my brother.' The prayer that made a prophet.
s.9a4a865d72ecb29b: 'We will strengthen your arm through your brother.' Partnership as divine gift.
s.294293724fc6e5b8: 'O son of my mother...' Gentleness under his brother's fury, for the sake of the people's unity.
s.20db5fba013bd5f0: Of the patient ones · Among Bani Israil, it is said
s.61e26738610e61da: Twice the Qur'an opens its registers of honor and includes a name wrapped in quiet: Dhul-Kifl. With Ismail and Idris he is counted 'of the patient' and admitted 'into Our mercy' (21:85-86); with Ismail and Alyasa he is 'of the excellent' (38:48). His very name means the possessor of a pledge or portion, and the commentators tell of a righteous man who guaranteed to fast the days, stand the nights, and judge the people without anger, and who kept the guarantee.
s.f64aeb705e9623d2: The Codex keeps to what the Book states: patience, righteousness, mercy, excellence. Some scholars count him a prophet, others a saint among Bani Israil. Either way his lesson is complete: heaven records the keepers of commitments, even when history loses their files.
s.e406a7a511ccd6db: 'And Ismail and Idris and Dhul-Kifl: all were of the patient.'
s.ae4c95d9b9dfbd63: 'And remember Ismail and Alyasa and Dhul-Kifl: all are among the excellent.'
s.0b6f343f502391cd: The iron-softening king · The kingdom of Bani Israil
s.57f6d070872e0962: He enters scripture as a shepherd boy in someone else's war. When the armies of Talut met Jalut's host, it was young Dawud who felled the giant, 'and Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom' (2:251). Kingship and prophethood met in one man, and neither corrupted the other.
s.0eadd5558e866a83: His gifts read like a psalm: the Zabur revealed to him (4:163); a voice so pure that 'We subjected the mountains to glorify with him, and the birds' (21:79); iron made soft in his hands, from which he crafted coats of mail, the armor-maker king who ate only from the work of his own hands. The Qur'an calls him awwab, ever returning to his Lord (38:17), and tells how two disputants climbed into his private chamber and their case, one ewe against ninety-nine, sent him falling into prostration, reading the parable against his own soul (38:24).
s.19beaaf8eb46ca82: 'And Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom.'
s.abba08a6b5568070: The mountains and birds subjected to echo his glorification.
s.361c60d3ad632791: 'O mountains, repeat with him, and the birds. And We softened iron for him.'
s.00ef480b33ed8e71: The parable of the ewes; the king falls in repentance, judged by his own verdict.
s.3bda26b208a1fce4: “The most beloved prayer to Allah is the prayer of Dawud, and the most beloved fasting is the fasting of Dawud: he slept half the night, stood a third, slept a sixth, and fasted every other day.”
s.e8e1a2c8f29ef12e: “Recitation was made easy for Dawud: he would order his mounts saddled and finish reciting before they were ready, and he ate only from the work of his own hands.”
s.64b932a79973cf19: The kingdom like no other after
s.73fff8d63b10c770: The kingdom like no other after · Son of Dawud
s.e459c52a1022e2d8: Sulayman inherited Dawud's throne and asked for something audacious: 'My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me' (38:35). It was granted in full. The wind ran errands of a month in a morning (34:12); jinn dove for pearls and built him sanctuaries and basins like reservoirs; molten copper flowed for him; and he was taught the speech of the birds (27:16).
s.bca1de39498fc703: The Qur'an's most beloved scene of him is small: an army of men, jinn and birds halts because one ant warned her colony to take cover. Sulayman smiled, amused at her words, and prayed the ruler's masterpiece: 'My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor... and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants' (27:19). Power that can hear an ant, and laughs, and immediately checks its own gratitude, is power passing its test.
s.5fbcac31e7f75033: With the hoopoe's report began the story of Saba: a sun-worshipping queen, a noble letter, a throne carried across the world in the blink of an eye by one with knowledge of the Book (27:40), and a hall of glass that led Bilqis from illusion to Islam: 'I submit, with Sulayman, to the Lord of the worlds' (27:44). His death was as instructive as his life: he remained standing on his staff, the jinn toiling on in fear, until a humble termite ate the stick and the great king fell, proving no one holds the unseen (34:14).
s.e7a4df851129141b: 'Grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me.' Asked, and given.
s.16df605b7dc95b35: 'We have been taught the language of the birds, and we have been given from all things.'
s.925d4faf3d3df1b9: He smiles at the ant's warning and prays for gratitude. The heart under the crown.
s.2e44efa1d3c933d7: The queen's throne brought before his glance returned; his reaction: 'this is from the favor of my Lord, to test me.'
s.5d08333570f3a61f: The staff, the termite, the fall: the jinn knew the unseen belongs to Allah alone.
s.9b9034b955047edf: Against the cult of Baal · Bani Israil after Sulayman
s.3442c59cb702c33e: Generations after Sulayman, Bani Israil bent toward a new idol with an old logic: Baal, god of rain and fertility, worshipped because the economy seemed to depend on him. Ilyas was sent with a question that dismantles every such bargain: 'Do you call upon Baal and abandon the best of creators: Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your first forefathers?' (37:125-126).
s.7925566a5a95a8ec: Most denied him, and the Qur'an notes their appointment with justice, then does for Ilyas what it does for its patient ones: it preserves his greeting forever. 'Peace upon Ilyas. Indeed, this is how We reward the doers of good' (37:129-131). A minority remembered; heaven remembered louder.
s.633c37196f7c87cf: 'Do you call upon Baal and abandon the best of creators?' The question that ends the rain-god bargain.
s.4cd69eb1cdf893cb: 'And We left for him among later generations: peace upon Ilyas.'
s.e4e32f49f8e4c51b: 'And Zakariyya and Yahya and Isa and Ilyas: all were of the righteous.'
s.1ed615c98d02600b: Of the excellent ones · After Ilyas
s.2dd3c665dfabe6ab: Alyasa carries the torch after Ilyas in the line of Bani Israil's prophets. The Qur'an names him twice, each time inside a list of honor: 'And Ismail and Alyasa and Yunus and Lut: each We preferred over the worlds' (6:86), and 'remember Ismail and Alyasa and Dhul-Kifl: all are among the excellent' (38:48).
s.00c7f018cb9a11fe: The tradition remembers him continuing Ilyas's stand against the Baal cult and shepherding the believers of his age. s.df688b2641ce1254: He was born in Makkah in the Year of the Elephant, around 570 CE, into the line of Ismail, orphaned of his father before birth and of his mother at six. The city that raised him gave him its highest civilian title before heaven gave him any: al-Amin, the Trustworthy. Merchants left him their deposits; rival clans chose his arbitration; when the Black Stone needed placing and swords were half-drawn over the honor, it was his cloak that carried it, with every clan holding an edge. He married Khadijah, fifteen years his employer before she was his wife, and for forty years lived so cleanly that when he later asked his city 'have you ever known me to lie?', not one enemy could say yes.
s.f768e192fd39ec64: At forty, in the cave of Hira above Makkah, the world changed weight. The angel Jibril seized him and the first word of the final revelation was a command that founded a civilization of readers: 'Iqra! Recite in the name of your Lord who created' (96:1). He came home trembling; Khadijah's answer is the first sentence of Muslim history: 'Never; by Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep the ties of kinship, carry the burdened, provide for the destitute, honor the guest, and help against the blows of fate.' Goodness, she reasoned, is not abandoned by its Author.
s.c0d48551085cb34f: Thirteen years in Makkah taught what the message costs. Bilal under the boulder, Sumayyah the first martyr, the boycott in the ravine eating leaves, the Year of Sorrow taking Khadijah and Abu Talib in one stretch, and Taif answering his gentlest offer with stones until his sandals ran red. Asked to curse the city, he answered: 'I hope Allah will bring from their descendants those who worship Him alone.' Then, in the hardest season, the gift: the Night Journey from Makkah to Jerusalem and the ascension through the heavens (17:1), where the five prayers were set as the believer's daily miraj.
s.7056f3ef494453c1: In 622 the emigration to Madinah turned a persecuted preacher into the builder of a civilization. From the cave where he calmed his companion, 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us' (9:40), he arrived to write a constitution between emigrants, helpers and tribes, to bond each Muhajir to an Ansari brother, and to raise a mosque whose floor was earth and whose reach would be the planet. Badr answered the years of torture with the day the Qur'an calls the Criterion (3:123); Uhud taught the price of one hill of disobedience; the Trench taught that endurance out-digs armies.
s.7a5ec82d9625317f: Then the strangest victory: a treaty that looked like surrender. At Hudaybiyyah he accepted terms his own companions could barely swallow, and the Qur'an named it 'a clear victory' (48:1). Peace proved the message's best amplifier: within two years more entered Islam than in all the prior nineteen. When Quraysh broke the treaty, he marched on Makkah with ten thousand and took his tormentor city without a battle, head bowed on his camel until his beard nearly touched the saddle. To the people who had starved, exiled and hunted him: 'Go, for you are free.' The conquest of Makkah remains history's most famous mass pardon.
s.401f295c582100ee: What remains is unmatched in human record: his sunnah preserved gesture by gesture, his Book letter by letter, his name joined to Allah's in every adhan on earth, every hour, without pause, and the promise of his station as the intercessor of the Day. The Qur'an does not call him a mercy to the Arabs, or to his century: 'We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds' (21:107). This entire Codex is one small lamp lit from that mercy.

s.268f6fa69cd67104: Thirty days that rearrange a year
s.bf68a7b0b1a8d542: Ramadan is the ninth month, the one in which the Qur’an was sent down, and the only month named in the Book. This room is built to be worth opening on the third day and on the twenty seventh: what today asks of you, where you are in the reading, what the last ten nights are for, and the plain mechanics nobody quite explains. Every date here is calculated and your masjid’s announcement is the one that counts.
s.cacae903095836b9: This room is open every day of the year and every word in it stays where it is. What changes is the interactive layer. About two weeks before the first of the month the preparation tools wake up and a countdown appears at the top. On the first of Ramadan everything wakes, and today becomes the first thing you see. After Eid the tools go back to resting and the knowledge stays exactly here, so a reader who arrives in October wanting to understand fasting is never turned away at the door.
s.afd814f33e4d6721: When a tool is resting it says so plainly, in its own place, and tells you the day it comes back. Nothing is hidden and nothing is disabled without explanation. The whole Codex follows the same calendar: a slim bar appears under the header as the month approaches, the site puts on a slight Ramadan theme for the thirty days, and at Eid the theme changes again and points at the Eid Room.
s.1571547cbbaff4ee: The dates here are calculated, not sighted. They come from the tabular Islamic calendar, which is arithmetic and has never once looked at the sky, so they can sit a day or two away from the day your community actually begins. Your masjid’s announcement is the date. If it differs from ours, move the calendar with the small offset control below and every time on this page follows you.
s.eb1787d0efd09ec2: Everything else carries its evidence in the open: a verse you can hear recited aloud, a narration named by its collection and number, and an honest badge whenever the scholars differ or a line is our own counsel rather than revelation. Where there is a real disagreement, both sides are given properly, because a reader who is told only one position has been handled rather than taught.

s.a36dea37d50f7cdd: The fast begins the moment true dawn enters, not at sunrise. That is why suhoor, the meal before dawn, is eaten late and finished close to the line.
s.725ccc4911c132cb: It ends the moment the sun is gone, and it is meant to be ended at once. Hastening the iftar is named as a good the community keeps.
s.67a91994206e8e66: The night belongs to you. Eat, drink, sleep, and be with your family without guilt: none of that was ever asked of you.
s.15e6a7456502cb8b: Eat and drink until the white thread of dawn becomes distinct to you from the black thread, then complete the fast until the night.

s.2de523d1b59b33bf: By the second day the stomach has stopped negotiating and started talking. Listen to it once, honestly. This is what somebody near you feels on an ordinary Tuesday with no Eid at the end of it. A fast that does not soften you toward the hungry has only made you thinner.
s.4d7b5eec7f1a886e: Whoever does not abandon false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need of him abandoning his food and drink. The tongue fasts as well, and it is far harder to hold than the jaw. If somebody picks a fight today, say I am fasting, and let the sentence end there.
s.46229b0d76ddff47: The month is not a long nap between two meals. Sleep enough to be kind to the people in your house, then spend the hours you saved from cooking and eating on something you will be glad to have done. The days are short and they do not come back.
s.ea4bde9e124cd458: Whoever gives a fasting person something to break his fast with has the same reward as him, and nothing is taken from the fasting person’s own reward. It does not have to be a banquet. A date and a cup of water is named in the report itself.
s.0ebfb751f5695daf: Your body has a claim on you
s.388e7859e237a907: The month of Ramadan is the one in which the Qur’an was sent down, guidance for the people. That is the month’s own reason for existing. Read a small amount every single day rather than a heroic amount once, because the small amount is the one that survives to the thirtieth.
s.63a4940a6b676448: Ask while your hands are open
s.a456dfa9ebb71ddb: And when My servants ask you about Me, I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me. That verse sits inside the fasting verses, not beside them. Keep a short list and read it in the last minutes before the adhan, when you are already waiting.
s.43d9bdb0f1745e42: A third of it is gone
s.b10e6c4bcd214f3d: Ten days have passed and you will not be given them back. Do not audit them with shame; shame is a poor engine and it stalls by the fifteenth. Choose one thing to do better for the next ten, write it somewhere you will actually see it, and leave the first ten alone.
s.75b78011508ecd57: The best prayer after the obligatory ones is the night prayer. It is the one act of worship with no audience at all, which is why it tells the truth about a person. Two units are enough to begin. Two units kept for twenty nights beats twenty units abandoned on the third.
s.c74a3fb1b23bb9f3: Let them pardon and overlook. Do you not love that Allah should forgive you? You are spending this month asking to be let off. Ask yourself honestly whether you are holding something over someone that is smaller than what you are asking Him to drop. Let it go today, quietly, without announcing it.
s.6b0c210e7d752764: The thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth of every month are the white days, named for the full moon that whitens the night. You are already fasting them this month without noticing. Note them now for the eleven months that follow, when fasting will be harder and worth more because nobody else is doing it.
s.56c973bac9e3d7a0: Half of it is behind you. Ask one question and answer it in one sentence: has anything actually changed in me, or have I only changed my meal times? If the answer is the second one, there is still half a month left, which is more than most people are given.
s.8806224e837c9dc8: The door with your parents’ name on it
s.0585c0069a992004: The parent is the middle door of paradise, so lose that door or guard it. Call them today and stay on the call after the news is finished. If they have died, this is the month to give on their behalf and to ask for them by name, out loud, so your own children hear you do it.
s.902639fb75da62e1: The strong one is not the one who throws people down. The strong one is the one who holds himself together at the moment of anger. Fasting takes away your usual comforts on purpose, which means every irritation arrives undefended. That is not the month failing. That is the training.
s.49857a3ed274bc10: On the seventeenth of Ramadan in the second year after the migration, a little over three hundred fasting men stood at Badr against three times their number, with the wrong equipment and no line of retreat. Allah had already given you victory at Badr while you were weak. Whatever you are afraid of today has been faced by someone with less.
s.91eb29ee9c845948: Jibril kept counselling me about the neighbour until I thought he would make him an heir. Ramadan is a loud month of cooking smells travelling along a corridor. Somewhere near you is a flat that smells of nothing. Send a plate, without a note, and do not wait to be thanked.
s.02e933f013e0474a: The last ten nights begin the night after tomorrow. Do the shopping now. Buy the gifts now. Settle the travel and the family arrangements now. It is a quiet tragedy to spend the most valuable nights of your year standing in a queue holding a basket.
s.0f55ac46d502ceb8: Seek it in the odd nights of the last ten. Tonight is the first of them. Nobody was told which night it is, and that hiding is deliberate: a person who knew the date would worship one night and sleep nine. You were made to search all ten.
s.fd23c3c615ef5e00: A thousand months is eighty three years and four months, which is a whole human life. One night has been placed inside your month that is worth more than all of it. Even the arithmetic alone should make a reasonable person sit up and rearrange the evening.

s.63caa63868ee691a: The plain of Arafah, the ninth of Dhul Hijjah
s.e244f8d0c03cacaa: One valley, one afternoon, the ninth of Dhul Hijjah in the year 10 AH. He rode into the middle of it so that the rings of listeners could face inward from every side.
s.927c251f8225b935: Criers were posted through the crowd to repeat each sentence outward, so the far rings heard the same words as the near ones.
s.c6998d145d380e2a: It was the largest gathering of his life, and the last time he would address it: about a hundred thousand pilgrims, most of whom would never see him again.
s.d28a742b9d3923e5: Jabir ibn Abdullah, who rode with him, preserved the fullest account of that day: the camel, the valley, the sermon, and the sun going down over the standing.

s.1441439a4eb8b6f0: He began where every narration of that day begins: ’Indeed your blood and your wealth are sacred to you, as sacred as this day of yours, in this month of yours, in this land of yours.’ His listeners measured holiness by three things above all: the day of Arafah, the month of Dhul-Hijjah, the precincts of the Haram.

s.1f47ab94d0ac0116: Read together, the sanctities he named at Arafah and at Mina form one fence with three bands around every believer: the life, the property, the good name. They are the sermon’s legal core, and the part of it that is quoted in courts and in khutbahs to this day.

s.61bf5106dbc4ca20: A note on the words red and black
s.9fcf16365a62d1d8: The sermon’s own wording is left exactly as it stands above. This note is only the meaning those two words carried in the ears that first heard them. In the Arabic of that century
s.f260e2c148647e4b: , ahmar, red, was how the Arabs named the light-skinned or white-skinned peoples, the Persians and the Byzantines among them; and
s.1d7c277c19ef608a: , aswad, black, named the dark-skinned peoples. Naming the two together was an idiom for the whole span of humanity, the way one might say from one end of the earth to the other.
s.0f11dbc895adcf5a: So the sentence is not weighing two tribes or two shades against each other in some narrow comparison. It gathers every human colour there is into one line and cancels the ranking of all of them at once, in the same breath that cancels the ranking of Arab over non-Arab. What is left standing as the only measure is taqwa, the mindfulness of Allah, which no lineage and no complexion can inherit or lose.

s.a1738c5a6a14ad48: The one journey every reader of this page will make
s.0dbf8d1bebca3195: The Qur’an and the Sunnah map this road in detail: the last breath, the leaving of the soul, the washing and the prayer of the living, the grave and its questioning, the long barzakh, the Trumpet, the gathering, the scales, the bridge and the two homes. None of it was revealed to frighten you, but so that a believer travels a road already drawn, toward a Lord already known, and so that grief, when it comes, has somewhere true to stand.
s.220fc69a17eeb968: If you have come here carrying a loss
s.479c7b4098611862: Read slowly, and take only what you can carry today. Nothing on this page was written to frighten you, and nothing here is a verdict on anyone you love: what happens to a particular soul is knowledge Allah kept for Himself, and the Sunnah forbids us from assigning anybody a seat in either home.
s.0c104f29d919c897: Every station below carries its evidence in the open, with an honest badge where the scholars differ or where a beloved report is weaker than it is usually presented. Where a narration is weak, this page says so instead of borrowing its comfort quietly.

s.d8fbd33cc4a1dc1a: One line, ten stations. Nothing on it is hidden from you: every stage below is named in the Qur’an or in authentic hadith, and this page walks them in order.
s.a09c2f7e39199840: The nodes light one after another because the journey is travelled that way, one station at a time, and never faster than Allah appoints.
s.d9a354d4c84b11e2: The thread does not end in a place you cannot reach. It ends at a fork, and the whole religion is about which branch a life was quietly leaning toward.
s.1ff89a74a8be079e: Behind them is a barrier until the day they are raised; then the Trumpet is blown; and faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.
s.d326683b8a91dadd: Nothing on this road happens early, and nothing happens late. ’Never will Allah delay a soul when its term has come.’ (63:11) ’It is not for any soul to die except by the permission of Allah, at a term appointed in writing.’ (3:145) The fixed term, the ajal, is among the most consoling doctrines given to the grieving: no accident, no illness, no delayed ambulance, no missed diagnosis took your beloved one hour before the writing.
s.2722fb67f0a2e4b1: It also quiets the living: guarding your life is commanded, but dread adds nothing to a term already set. ’Say: indeed the death from which you flee will surely meet you.’ (62:8) The question the Qur’an leaves open is never whether, only in what state you will be met.
s.9e0f68f4043afe2e: If you are turning over what might have been done differently, the Qur’an answers before you finish the sentence: the term was written, and it was never yours to move. What is still yours is the du’a, the supplication, that you can make for them tonight.
s.413198f14046fe4b: The long hadith of al-Bara ibn Azib, recorded in Musnad Ahmad and Abu Dawud and graded sahih by many scholars of hadith, is the fullest single map of the crossing. Angels with faces like the sun descend and sit before the dying believer, bringing a shroud and perfume from Paradise. The Angel of Death says: ’O good soul, come out to forgiveness from Allah and His pleasure.’
s.e1015cae4fd19d94: And the soul flows out ’as a drop flows from the mouth of a waterskin.’ For the one who spent life denying his Lord, the same moment reverses: ’O foul soul, come out to the displeasure and anger of Allah,’ and it is dragged out ’as a skewer is drawn through wet wool.’ Death is one event; dying is two experiences.
s.04897deddea56543: The same narration follows the soul upward. Wrapped in its shroud of Paradise, the believer’s soul gives off ’the finest musk found on the face of the earth,’ and every company of angels it passes asks: ’Who is this good soul?’
s.9a2244d3f42e0bd9: They answer with the most beautiful of the names he was called in the world, and the gate of each heaven opens, and the angels nearest to Allah in every heaven escort him to the next, up to the seventh, where the command is given: ’Write My servant’s record in Illiyyin,’ and the soul is returned to the body for the questioning. The other soul rises with a stench, is announced by its ugliest names, and for it, as the Qur’an had already said, ’the gates of heaven will not be opened.’ (7:40)
s.1eb9f482884d21b0: Two souls leave the same way and meet two different receptions, and the difference is not made at the end. It is made in ordinary weeks, in what a person kept saying and doing when nothing was at stake.
s.9bd305adc57661bf: What the Living Owe the Body
s.f0efb611f8dddcb3: The body that carried a soul is not waste to be disposed of. It is a trust with rights, and the community around it owes four: al ghusl, the washing; al kafan, the shrouding; salat al janazah, the prayer over it; and al dafn, the burial. They are fard kifayah, a duty on the community as a whole, which means that if nobody does them everybody has sinned, and once enough hands take them up the rest are released.
s.60295a3b481a1dcd: Every instruction points the same direction: modesty, gentleness, speed without hurry, no display and no expense. He taught that the funeral should be carried without delay, and he forbade the wailing and the tearing of clothes that the age of ignorance had made into theatre. The last kindness a person receives from human hands is meant to be quiet.

s.4d53d62e0e488fac: A Pen in the House of Judgment
s.16ae92de0f5b7350: Baghdad in those years was the heaviest city in the world, and the busiest, and the loudest at noon: the round city of the caliphs aging at its center, the markets of Karkh roaring on the west bank, the Tigris between them carrying rafts of skins loaded with dates, tar, pottery, soldiers, melons, grief, everything. Paper had come to the city within living memory, and the city had fallen on it like a hungry man on bread. There were mills for it now, and a street of sellers, and in the offices of the state the scratching of pens had become the sound of power itself.
s.33063f998278881b: Thabit was a porter’s son from the Karkh side who had been caught, at nine years old, writing the names of dates in the dust of his father’s stall in a hand so clean that a passing teacher stopped and stared. The kuttab, the boys’ school, took him for the sake of that hand. The offices took him at seventeen. By twenty he was a junior katib, a scribe, in the court of a qadi, a judge, and he loved the work the way some men love the sea, without being able to say why the love went so deep.
s.3dbc7015ea96032b: It was his teacher, an old scribe with one clouded eye, who had set the nail in him years before. Paper forgets nothing, the old man said. So write nothing on it that wants forgetting, and never once make it lie. A lying page outlives its liar, and stands up on the Day the scrolls are laid open, and reads itself aloud. Thabit was thirteen when he heard that. Some sentences arrive before the life they are meant for, and wait.
s.47a4eae54e846563: His work was the mahdar, the written minute of what was said in court: claim, answer, testimony, oath. Above it stood the sijill, the judgment enrolled and sealed. He wrote quickly and exactly, and he believed with his whole young heart that the room he served was a scale, and the qadi’s pen its needle, and that between the ink and the truth there ran a marriage no power in Baghdad could divorce.
s.586df8ed963d719f: The qadi he served was old, learned, and tired, with thirty years of honest judgments in small matters behind him. He was honest the way most men are honest: in the amounts that cost little. This is not a rare kind of man. It is the commonest kind there is, and no one knows which kind he himself is until the day the amount is large.
s.0ce2c2ab46d1a4ad: Around the court moved the other Baghdad, the one that does not appear in the minutes: chamberlains of great houses, cousins of cousins, notes folded small and sealed with important rings, witnesses of professional reputation. The court kept a roll of men certified as udul, upright, whose word the law would accept. Udul is the plural of adl, justice; the word and the Name are kin. The court called those men just. Remember the roll of the upright, and remember what the word means, for this story turns on the distance between a word and its meaning.
s.34b23a3ce356b626: Dawud the date seller had a stall in Karkh no wider than a prayer mat and a voice that could reach across the whole date market: amber ones, honey ones, black ones from my own palms, sweetness with a Bismillah in it. The sweetness was not a boast. He owned sixty palms on a canal below the city, planted by his father, and at day’s end he gave the bruised fruit to the porters’ children free, and everyone in that market had at some time been small, and remembered him.
s.7c6b7e6e83b4adb0: The orchard had water on two sides, and shade, and a view down the running canal, and it was therefore beautiful, and it was therefore seen. The man who saw it had a cousin who kept the door of a palace, a stronger form of wealth in Baghdad than land. He offered Dawud a price that was an insult wearing the clothes of an offer. Dawud said: my father put sixty shoots into this ground with Bismillah over every one of them; find me the price of sixty Bismillahs and I will consider it. He said it mildly, and the market repeated it for a month, laughing warmly. It was the most expensive sentence of his life.
s.5eb26927b3878bc9: The claim, when it came, was beautiful in its workmanship. A deed of sale, twenty years old by its date: the orchard sold to the claimant’s late father by Dawud’s late father, price received in full, possession deferred by family arrangement. Two witnesses from the roll of the udul, men with certified beards and certified reputations, stood forth and swore they had seen the signing with their own eyes, twenty years past. Dawud stood in the court with his mouth open, holding a water skin he had forgotten he was holding, and his one witness was an old neighbor who stammered under the eyes of the room and got a date wrong, and was dismissed.
s.a03a425053722656: It fell to Thabit to copy the deed into the mahdar, and this is where the case entered him like a blade, because paper was his craft and ink was his mother tongue. The deed claimed twenty years. But the sheet was of the smooth new stock the mill by the Syrian Gate had been making for less than a decade; he had a ream of its brothers on his own shelf.
s.55a23e84688a94fa: And the ink. Gall ink is a living thing; it goes down black and then browns with the years toward rust, like iron, like blood. This ink was black as the state’s own banners, black as a crow in the rain. The folds were sharp. The worm had not found it. The deed was a young man wearing his grandfather’s turban, and to Thabit’s trained eyes it might as well have been laughing.
s.c1876f6789a0b53d: He went to the qadi at day’s end, privately, as a junior should, and laid the sheet in the lamplight and said what he saw, item by item, the paper, the ink, the folds, in the flat voice of his trade.
s.4bc47fdda1a08237: The qadi looked at the deed for a long time, and at the folded note with an important seal that lay on his own table, and then at nothing. The witnesses are certified, he said at last. Certification is the court’s eyes; I cannot see past my own instruments. Copy the record, Thabit. And then, softer, being for one moment merely an old man: they would not stop at taking my post. I have daughters. You will understand when the world has given you more to lose.
s.1fd6c161b60e1aef: Thabit walked home along the canal through the smell of evening bread, and told his wife, because he told her everything. She was quiet while he spoke. Their daughter slept in the corner with a fist against her cheek. We ate barley before you served in that court, his wife said finally, which was her whole argument and both sides of it. Then she said the sentence he carried to his grave: do what you can pray behind.
s.2f6f9c00fc46a6f2: Judgment was given on a Thursday, in a full room, the claimant’s people in linen worth more than the orchard’s year, Dawud in washed cotton with his hands empty. The witnesses swore again, smooth as pulleys. The qadi ruled the deed proven and the orchard passed, and the room made the small sound rooms make when a thing everyone predicted has finished happening: not a gasp, only a settling, like poured grain.
s.31e2c81f361f5889: Then the clerk of the court was to enroll the judgment, and the clerk of the court did not move. Thabit sat with the reed in his hand and the sijill open before him, and the room waited, and he heard his own voice arrive from a distance, level, as if dictating to itself: I cannot write that this court found the truth. I copied the deed. Its paper is younger than my daughter, and its ink is younger than her teeth. Let the record show the witnesses certified and the paper new, and let whoever reads it weigh both.
s.61391ad118424f93: For a moment the room was perfectly still, and in that stillness something very old and very large seemed to lean over it and look in.
s.1270e47adc1c8734: What happened then happened quickly, the way such things do. He was removed from the room by two bailiffs, not roughly, the way you remove a lamp that is smoking. Another hand enrolled the sijill before the ink was dry. Within the week his name was struck from the diwan lists, every office of the state closed to him at a single stroke, and a soft voiced man he had never met stood beside him in the mosque courtyard and observed that a scribe who will not write is a knife that will not cut, and that both go into the drawer, and that he should thank Allah it was only the drawer. Thabit thanked Allah, though not for that.
s.c7c02651804d5b5f: The judgment stood. Understand this, because the story will not soften it later: it stood. It stands, as far as the records of this world run, to this day.
s.c6ac5dfea90aac44: The orchard’s fate was quick. Within two years the new owner had felled forty of the sixty palms, because palms drop dates and dates draw wasps and wasps trouble guests, and had raised a pavilion of cedar with rose plots to the water’s edge, and hung lamps in the trees that were left, whose fruit no one picked. Pleasure boats tied there at night, and the music carried across the canal to the road where the fruit carts passed.
s.0af2a71603637df0: Dawud carried loads in the date market until his back bent, and died in a fever year, and was buried in the common ground, with a date palm frond laid on the bier by the porters’ children, who had grown, and remembered.
s.6c3718843705c1ba: For Thabit there began the years of barley bread. No diwan would touch him; the stroke that struck his name had been thorough. He set a reed mat by the gate of a Friday mosque and became a letter writer, a young man among the old men of that trade, taking dictation from mothers whose sons had gone for soldiers in Khurasan, drawing up bills of sale for onion men, marriage lists for brides whose fathers counted the dowry twice. He was paid in copper fals, sometimes in eggs, once a winter cloak. He wrote each letter as if it were a sijill of the empire, because exactness was the one wealth no one could strike from any list.
s.8a79f8129cf4737c: Poverty is not dramatic; that is its power. It is barley instead of wheat, one lamp lit only for the Qur’an and mending done twice, a daughter married with a dowry raised by selling the good brass pen case, a wife whose hands took in spinning and whose mouth never once, in forty years, said the words you could have stayed silent. Once he asked her outright if she regretted the day the pen refused. She was quiet the length of three breaths. I regret the pavilion, she said. I do not regret you. Eat your bread.
s.3e935a84fe370d8a: For six years he went to the mazalim, the court of complaints where the wronged of the empire could in principle hand their grievance upward past every corrupted instrument. He stood in lines among men who had walked from other provinces holding petitions like sick children. Twice his paper was taken, stamped, and drowned somewhere upstream. Once a young clerk he had himself trained avoided his eyes with such labor that Thabit pitied him and left the line. Petitions rose in that office the way water rises: they did not. In the seventh year he stopped going, not because his certainty had died, but because he finally understood the address was wrong.
s.a880b587aa1f5691: The man whose cousin kept the palace door lived long, gave banquets, and built at a crossroads of Karkh a public fountain, from which the quarter drank and called him generous. Thabit passed that fountain on foot for thirty years. Once, in a hot Ramadan twilight, to teach his heart something he could not name, he made himself drink from it, and stood with the sweet water on his lips while the man’s carved name looked down at him from the stone. He was never sure what the lesson had been, only that his heart came away from it quieter, the way a fever breaks in the night without anyone seeing the hour.
s.e5405f8baab6cf39: But do not let the quietness deceive you; there was a war in him, and it lasted years. There were nights he laid his forehead on the mat and could not find one word to send up, nights he asked outright: where was Your court, ya Rabb, my Lord, when the only door above that door was Yours? You saw the ink. You made the eyes I saw it with.
s.44cc72a4c608ece2: No answer came. What came, in its own time, was the ordinary dawn: the adhan over the roofs, bread, his wife’s hand on his shoulder, the pen to be cut, the mat to be swept. He understood nothing more than before. He was held no less than before. He learned, slowly, the difference between an answer and a floor, and that the second is what a man actually stands on, all his life.
s.85b2d323980230d9: The Record That Does Not Smudge
s.049eb9a821054f4a: One thing he had done, the night of the judgment, and told no one but his wife. He had sat till the lamp burned out and written, in his exact court hand, a full and true record of the case: the claim, the deed, the paper of the deed, the ink of the deed, the folds, the names of the witnesses from the roll of the upright, what was said in the lamplight and by whom, and the judgment as it was enrolled by another hand.
s.4e9b534a580c892c: He sealed it in a reed tube against damp, and set it in a niche of the wall, and waited for the reviewing qadi, the honest successor, the day of the reopened file. Qadis came and went. The wrong outlived them all, as wrongs bred in high places do; they are hardy stock. The tube stayed in the wall forty years, and he called it, privately, his second record.
s.0efb105a04e3ea94: In his old age his hands took the shake, and his daughter’s son, Ayyub, a sharp boy with his grandfather’s exact eyes, learned the pen beside him at the mosque gate and grew furious with the story when he was old enough to be told it. The heirs of that house still hold the land, the boy said. Take out the tube. There are new offices now, new men, I will carry it myself.
s.941070ce7fe09fb4: Thabit looked at his grandson with the long look of a man counting what a thing will cost the person he loves, and said: the men who did it are all before Allah already, and the men who hold it now bought roses, not palms; they know nothing. And then, seeing the boy’s face: you think I am letting the wrong die. Sit down, and I will show you where it is kept.
s.aabf01eb851e72cd: He took the tube to the river at dawn, the boy beside him carrying the wudu jug, past the fountain with the dead man’s name on it, down to the brown Tigris where the rafts went by loaded with dates from someone’s palms somewhere. He broke the seal and read it over once, the whole of it, in a steady voice, to the water and the boy and the gulls, the way the record of a case is read before a judge.
s.a2943934425a2a1e: Then he said: I wrote what happened. So did One who does not smudge. Mine has waited fifty years for a judge with clean hands. His does not wait; it is already entered, and the session is already appointed, and the witnesses cannot be bought, for the witnesses are the skins of the accused themselves.
s.937f5c6c54ffe866: He let the river take the paper. It rode the current a little way, turning, pale on the brown water, and went under without ceremony, and nothing fell out of the world. That is what the boy said he remembered best, telling it years later as an old scribe himself: that he had braced himself to feel the truth drown, and instead felt the morning become very wide and very light, as if a debt had been transferred to a House that could carry it, and the porters released.
s.a7ec80bfdd871a41: They prayed Fajr on the bank, the old man and the boy, on one spread cloak. In the prostration Thabit stayed down a long time, and Ayyub, glancing sideways as boys do, saw the old lips moving and thought he was pleading, and only understood decades later that he had been doing the other thing: he had been handing something over, item by item, palms and pavilion and fountain and pen, into the custody of the only Court that had never once lost his respect.
s.2c06f2d9f69eb023: He died poor, in the month of Shaban, owing no one, owed by this world more than it ever paid. The mosque of the gate where he had written letters for forty years could not hold the janazah crowd, which would have astonished him: mothers of soldiers, onion men, porters, brides grown grey, a whole city of small correct documents come walking behind their scribe.
s.9374d785da1b660b: There was no vindication in it. The orchard is a garden of someone else’s roses to this day, and no record in any office of this world says otherwise. The scales of Baghdad went on weighing short, as the scales of every Baghdad do. And above the whole patient city, unhurried, unbought, exact to the weight of a mustard seed, the other Court kept its records, and kept its appointment. It keeps them still.
s.1afa04ae912eb184: Ask why the scribe was never repaid, and you have asked the question the story cannot answer and the Name can. Al-Adl does not mean the One who makes every court honest by Thursday. It means the One before whom every Thursday is still open, every file recoverable, every mustard seed weighed: the Judge who was never for one instant deceived, and never for one instant late, whose session no cousin can enter through the side door, because the Judge has no cousins, and His house has no side doors.
s.ffc8ac9b762335a5: And We will set the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, and no soul will be wronged in anything. And if there be the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth. And sufficient are We as reckoners.
